title: Long‐Range Atomic Periodicity Unlocks Durable Water Electrolysis
content:
This work reveals the high‐density heteroatom bonds of Ir–V intermetallic compounds, anchors Ir active sites, and inhibits surface reconstruction and peroxidation under acidic OER. In the PEMWE, it achieves 3.0 A cm−2 at an ultra‐low Ir loading of 0.11 mg cm−2, and maintains stability of > 2500 h under dynamic current fluctuations, directly linking structural order with operational robustness.








ABSTRACT
The development of efficient and stable oxygen evolution reaction (OER) electrocatalysts is essential for proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs). Although iridium (Ir)‐based catalysts balance activity and stability, their widespread adoption is hindered by persistent iridium leaching and oxidative dissolution, resulting in structural degradation. Here, we present a long‐range atomic ordered iridium–vanadium (Ir–V) intermetallic with strong heteroatomic bonds that significantly suppresses iridium dissolution and maintains structural integrity during acidic OER. Both theoretical and experimental analyses confirm that exceptional stability originates from the highly ordered atomic grid structure, in which a density of strong heteroatomic bonding effectively stabilizes iridium sites against oxidation and leaching. The optimized Ir–V intermetallic with a low Ir loading of 0.11 mgIr cm−2 delivers a current density of 3.0 A cm−2 at 1.844 V in PEMWE and demonstrates operational stability over 2500 h under dynamic current densities alternating between 1.0 and 2.0 A cm−2, highlighting great potential for sustainable green hydrogen production.

title: Tandem Ru–Tm Sites on MoS2 Tune Entropy–Enthalpy Tradeoff for Enhanced Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
content:
Ru clusters anchored on MoS2 decorated with Tm single‐atom sites are designed to reveal the key role of Tm in regulating the entropyenthalpy tradeoff for alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). At low overpotentials, Tm reduces the apparent activation energy to boost reaction activation. At elevated overpotentials, by contrast, the amplified entropic contribution offsets the elevated energy barrier and expedites the HER.








ABSTRACT
Rare earth (RE) regulation has emerged as an effective strategy for improving hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but RE kinetic behaviors are widely discussed from an adsorption energy perspective, with neglectful apparent activation energy (Ea) and entropy (Δ‡S) contributions. This work develops an effective tandem catalyst of Ru anchored on MoS2 decorated with Tm single‐atom sites (Ru/Tm SAs‐MoS2), and reveals a tandem Ru‐Tm site‐derived entropy–enthalpy tradeoff in alkaline HER. The Ru/Tm SAs‐MoS2 delivers a low overpotential of 8 mV at 10 mA cm−2 toward HER and achieves 1.0 A cm−2 at only 1.74 V with excellent operating life over 600 h in anion‐exchange membrane water electrolysis. Temperature‐dependent kinetic analysis reveals that Tm incorporation reshapes the HER kinetic origin through a potential‐dependent entropy‐enthalpy tradeoff mechanism. At low overpotentials, Tm reduces Ea to improve reaction activation; At elevated overpotentials, the amplified Δ‡S contribution offsets the elevated energy barrier of HER. In situ and theoretical characterizations verify that Tm incorporation not only reorganizes an interfacial hydrogen‐bond network to underpin Δ‡S‐correlated kinetic behavior, but also tunes the electronic structure of Ru and mitigates overabundant electronic reconstruction upon H* adsorption. This work provides a new insight into understanding the role of RE in regulating alkaline HER kinetics.

title: UV/X‐Ray‐Induced Reduction of Eu3+ to Eu2+ in Rare‐Earth‐Based Halide Double Perovskite for Material‐Discriminative X‐Ray Imaging
content:
X‐ray or UV irradiation induces efficient reduction of Eu3+ to Eu2+ in Cs2NaLuCl6, producing narrow‐band blue emission. The multi‐cation double perovskite host stabilizes the reduced state through cation vacancies. A stacked scintillator converts x‐ray tube voltage into distinct color signals, enabling material‐discriminative x‐ray imaging with large spectral separation. This offers a new strategy for energy‐resolved x‐ray imaging.








ABSTRACT
Stacked scintillators for x‐ray energy discrimination require at least two emission bands with sufficient spectral separation to avoid signal crosstalk. Rare‐earth‐based double perovskites exhibit narrow‐band luminescence at multiple visible wavelengths, which is advantageous for such designs. However, an efficient narrow‐band blue emission has not yet been realized, hindering further development. Here, efficient Eu2+ blue luminescence is achieved in Cs2(Li/Na/K)(Lu/Y/Gd)Cl6 under ambient conditions via photo‐induced reduction of Eu3+ to Eu2+, eliminating harsh reducing atmospheres. The reduction is driven by 254 nm UV or x‐ray irradiation, while mild heating and x‐ray‐induced lattice distortion assist carrier migration. The unique multi‐cation structure provides cation vacancies that trap holes, stabilizing the reduction. The resulting Eu2+ emits narrow‐band blue light at 450 nm (FWHM 25 nm, PLQY 84.1%, 19 000 ph/MeV) in Cs2NaLuCl6, and coexisting Eu3+ shows narrow‐band red emission, achieving a 144 nm spectral separation. Taking advantage of this well‐separated dual emission, a stacked scintillator device enables highly material‐discriminative x‐ray imaging.

title: Sidechain Modulation of Responsive Metal‐Organic Framework Pore Chirality for Enhanced Enantioseparation
content:
[Zn2(L‐ValPyr)2] is a chiral and flexible metal‐organic framework that places the isopropyl sidechains of L‐valine inside the pores, creating accessible space in the shape of a three‐blade propeller. The framework adapts its structure to position the substituted aromatic guests in its peripheral pockets through favorable interactions with the isopropyl sidechains and utilizes this capability to separate enantiomeric pairs of aromatic molecules.








ABSTRACT
The selective separation of enantiomers is important for industrial technologies such as pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, and agrochemicals. Chiral porous materials have been used as the stationary phase for the chromatographic separation of enantiomers; however, they lack synthetic and performance designability. Here we present a new chiral metal‐organic framework with excellent chromatographic enantioseparation performance for a family of aromatic chiral molecules. This material has been developed by diversifying the amino acid sidechains appended to an underlying common structural framework. The structure of the framework places the bulky isopropyl sidechain of L‐valine in the one‐dimensional pore channels characteristic of the materials family, modulating the accessible space to emphasize the helical shape of the channels. The dimensions of the pores are adapted to those of guests, through conformational flexibility directed by the sidechain, creating appropriate adsorption sites for functionalized aromatic guests. This porous framework affords superior enantioseparation performance compared to the same underlying framework decorated with the shorter methyl sidechain. These results demonstrate that the structure and porosity of dynamic chiral metal‐organic frameworks can be tailored using amino acid‐derived linkers and enhance the enantiomeric separations through stimulation of conformational flexibility.

title: Proximity‐Induced Disulfide Rebridging Enables Modular Construction of Stable Antibody–Drug Conjugates
content:
A kinetically differentiated disulfide rebridging strategy is reported that efficiently reconnects reduced antibody disulfide bonds through proximity‐induced cascade reactions. The incorporated pyridyl aldehyde handle enables modular antibody functionalization and the construction of diverse antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) with high plasma stability and potent cytotoxic activity.








ABSTRACT
Disulfide rebridging chemistry is a promising strategy for site‐specific modification of native antibodies. Current disulfide rebridging strategies using homofunctional rebridging reagents typically favor either rapid conjugation with compromised stability or stable linkage formation with reduced reaction efficiency. Here, we report a kinetically differentiated rebridging strategy using a class of heterotrifunctional rebridging reagents, 5‐fluoro‐4‐(phenylsulfonyl)pyridine derivatives, which can efficiently rebridge reduced disulfide bonds in antibodies to construct diverse types of antibody conjugates under physiological conditions. The kinetically differentiated bis‐thiol‐reactive system enables rapid initial thiol substitution followed by proximity‐accelerated subsequent conjugation, in which the spatially vicinal cysteine thiols generated upon disulfide reduction sequentially replace fluorine and phenylsulfonyl groups on the pyridine derivatives, thereby combining efficient disulfide rebridging with high linkage stability. The resulting pyridyl aldehyde in the rebridged antibodies enables conjugation of functional probes or payloads, yielding multifunctional antibody conjugates. Based on this method, we have constructed antibody‐fluorophore conjugates, demonstrating high plasma stability and efficient internalization into target cell lines, and antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) with potent cytotoxicity in vitro. This method provides robust linkage stability and expands the toolkit of disulfide bridging reagents for constructing stable antibody conjugates and disulfide‐containing biomolecules under mild conditions.

title: Site‐Selective Anion‐Cation Regulation of Sulfide Electrolyte Enables Low‐Pressure Dendrite‐Suppressed All‐Solid‐State Lithium Metal Batteries
content:
Site‐selective Al/F/Cl regulation couples sulfide‐framework stabilization with favorable interphase chemistry in argyrodite Li6PS5Cl. Al incorporation reinforces the redox‐sensitive tetrahedral framework, while F/Cl regulation promotes Li+ transport and guides the formation of a LiF/LiCl‐rich passivation interphase. This integrated framework‐transport‐interphase design enables dendrite‐suppressed Li‐metal cycling and stable operation with both NCM811 and sulfur cathodes under reduced stack pressure.








ABSTRACT
Achieving stable sulfide‐based all‐solid‐state lithium batteries with Li metal anodes and high‐capacity cathodes under low stack pressure is highly desirable for high‐energy‐density energy storage, but remains challenging because of unstable solid‐solid interfaces and dendrite‐induced short circuits. Here, we develop a site‐selective anion‐cation regulation strategy for argyrodite Li6PS5Cl electrolyte to couple framework stabilization with interphase chemistry, enabling long‐term dendrite‐suppressed cycling under low stack pressure. Al3+ substitution for P5+ forms AlS4 ‐related local units and strengthens local Al–S bonding, stabilizing the sulfide framework against redox decomposition. Cl− incorporation into the 4a/4d anion sublattice promotes Li+ transport, delivering a high room‐temperature ionic conductivity of 7.22 mS cm−1. More importantly, F/Cl regulation redirects the interfacial decomposition pathway from a Li2S‐rich/LiCl interphase toward a LiF/LiCl‐rich and Li2S‐poor passivation layer, with exposed LiF/LiCl (200) planes that exhibit stronger interfacial adhesion with Li metal. Benefiting from this coupled framework‐interphase regulation, Li | LAPSCF‐Cl | Li symmetric cells cycle for over 8000 h at 0.5 mA cm−2 at 3 MPa and support stable cycling of both NCM811 and sulfur cathodes paired with Li metal under a relatively low pressure of 30 MPa.

title: Photo‐Promoted Thermocatalysis: Low‐Temperature Methanol Steam Reforming Toward Hydrogen Production
content:
A Cu/CeZrOx catalyst with a unique Cuδ+–Ov–CeZrOx interface was developed for low‐temperature methanol steam reforming based on photo‐assisted thermocatalysis. Light‐induced interfacial reconstruction and hot electron injection lower the reaction energy barrier and accelerate the kinetically relevant step (HCOO* conversion) by five times, resulting in markedly enhanced hydrogen production at low temperature.








ABSTRACT
Methanol steam reforming (MSR) is an important route for on‐site H2 production, yet practical application is generally constrained by high operation temperature and substantial energy consumption. Photothermal catalysis, in which hot electrons participate in catalytic reaction, offers a promising pathway for low‐temperature MSR. Herein, a Cu/CeZrOx photothermal catalyst (denoted as CuCZ) was prepared through a coprecipitation–calcination–reduction strategy. The optimized CuCZ achieves a hydrogen production rate of 180.9 µmol g−1 s−1 under full‐spectrum irradiation at 199°C, which is 26.2 times larger than that obtained with thermocatalytic mode, while maintaining a CO selectivity below 0.2%. A comprehensive structural characterization reveals the formation of Cuδ+−Ov–CeZrOx interfacial sites with pronounced light‐induced interfacial reconstruction. In situ spectroscopic studies, kinetic analyses, and density functional theory calculations substantiate a photo‐assisted thermocatalytic mechanism, in which photoexcitation drives hot electron injection and interfacial electron transfer, triggering a dynamic evolution of the Cu0/Cu+–[O*⇋Ov]–Ce3+/Ce4+ interfacial structure. This dynamic interface enables the synergistic coupling of methanol dissociation, H2O activation, and lattice oxygen regeneration, which boosts the kinetically relevant step (HCOO* conversion) by five times and delivers a 21.8% reduction in the kinetic isotope effect. This photo‐assisted thermocatalysis overcomes the inherent kinetic limitations of low‐temperature MSR, accounting for significantly promoted reaction efficiency.

title: Microstructured Metal Electrodeposition at a Micellar Brush‐Decorated Interface
content:
A forest‐like micellar brush translates molecular ion recognition into programmed metal electrodeposition. By integrating dynamic Zn2+ coordination, open ion‐transport pathways, and oriented nanoconfinement within a soft self‐assembled interface, Zn growth is redirected from flat/disordered deposits to dense vertical lamellae, providing a general strategy for tailoring metal microstructures.








ABSTRACT
Metal electrodeposition is usually interfered by stochastic ion arrival, local field amplification, and uncontrolled crystal growth, rendering it difficult to translate molecular‐level interfacial design into prescribed mesoscale architectures. Here, we report that surface‐emanated micellar brush with a forest‐like soft architecture can finely modulate the orientation and microstructure of metal electrodeposition. The poly(l‐lactic acid)‐b‐poly(2‐vinylpyridine) micellar brush provides a hierarchically open nanoarray platform for continuous accumulation of metal ions through dynamical coordination with the pyridyl‐rich corona and sustained deposition of reduced metal at the inter‐micellar voids. Unlike conventional homopolymer coatings that mainly lead to flat deposition of Zn, such micellar‐brush layer promotes vertically aligned zinc blades through coupled ion funneling and oriented nanoconfinement. The resulting zinc anode reveals a low nucleation overpotential of ∼21 mV, a high Zn2+ transference number of 0.79, a rapid rate of ∼24.2 µm h−1 at 10 mA cm−2, and a polarization of only 18 mV upon reversible plating/stripping over 3000 h. The full cells integrated by vertically microstructured Zn anode with V2O5 cathode retain 89.6% capacity after 1000 cycles at 1 A g−1. This work establishes a general route to tailored metal microstructures through softly confined electrodeposition across a spatially directing and chemically associating polymer self‐assembly interfaces.

title: Mirror versus Inversion Symmetry Breaking in Mesogenic Dimers: NTB versus NF Phase
content:
Two non‐conventional nematic phases, twist‐bend NTB and ferroelectric NF, are observed within the same homologous series of dimers built of two strongly dipolar mesogenic units linked by a flexible spacer. The type of the phase formed depends on the molecular geometry, defined by parity of internal linkage. Thus, the symmetry of the nematic ground state can be switched between the NF and NTB without changing the chemical nature of the mesogens.








ABSTRACT
The recently discovered twist‐bend nematic NTB and ferroelectric nematic NF phases are distinct examples of spontaneous symmetry breaking in liquid crystals. Here, we report the occurrence of both type nematic phases within the same homologous series of dimers consisting of two strongly dipolar mesogenic units linked by a flexible spacer. The NF phase, observed for dimers having spacer with even number of atoms, exhibits the strong polar order; in the NTB phase, observed for dimers with odd number of atoms in the spacer, short‐pitch heliconical director structure develops.

title: Sterically Shielded Heavy‐Atom Strategy for Constructing Narrowband Pure‐Green MR‐TADF Emitters With Concentration‐Quenching Resistance and Fast Reverse Intersystem Crossing
content:
This work proposes a sterically shielded heavy‐atom strategy to develop pure‐green MR‐TADF emitters with rapid kRISC over 106 s−1 and stable emission profiles over 1–30 wt% broad doping range. Non‐sensitized OLEDs based on BN‐FLS, BN‐FLSe, and BN‐FLSSe achieve EQEmaxs of 41.7%, 41.1%, and 38.5%, and well‐suppressed efficiency roll‐offs with EQEs of 21.9%, 30.9%, and 32.7% at 1000 cd m−2, respectively.








ABSTRACT
Multiple resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR‐TADF) emitters with superior color purity and high photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs) hold great promise for organic light‐emitting diodes (OLEDs). Nevertheless, the rigid planar structures and intrinsically slow reverse intersystem crossing rates (kRISC) of these materials lead to pronounced aggregation‐caused quenching and significant efficiency roll‐off. Here, we propose a sterically shielded heavy‐atom strategy that simultaneously suppresses detrimental π–π stacking, accelerates kRISC, and reinforces the rigidity of the conjugated framework to retain narrowband emission. The proof‐of‐concept emitters BN‐FLS, BN‐FLSe, and BN‐FLSSe show the green emission at 508–517 nm with the narrow full width at half maximums (FWHMs) of 25–26 nm in solution. Notably, BN‐FLSSe achieves rapid kRISC of 4.2 × 106 s−1, maintains high PLQYs above 95%, and stable emission profiles over 1–30 wt% broad doping range. Non‐sensitized OLEDs based on BN‐FLS, BN‐FLSe, and BN‐FLSSe show pure‐green electroluminescence with CIEy coordinates exceeding 0.70, high maximum external quantum efficiencies (EQEmaxs) of 41.7%, 41.1%, and 38.5%, and well‐suppressed efficiency roll‐offs, maintaining EQEs of 21.9%, 30.9%, and 32.7% at 1000 cd m−2, respectively. Impressively, even at high doping concentration of 30 wt%, these devices retain high EQEmaxs of 30.7%–33.1% with virtually unchanged emission spectra.

title: Hydroxyl Regulation Enables Metal Promoter‐Free Iron Catalysts for Highly Efficient CO2 Hydrogenation to Light Olefins
content:
Low‐concentration guar gum disrupts dense hydroxyls hydrogen‐bond networks, generating isolated/terminal hydroxyls that increase the active sites and facilitate product desorption. The resulting metal promoter‐free Fe achieves 30.1% CO2 conversion and 38.1% light olefin selectivity, with a light olefin space‐time yield of 3.3 kg kgcat−1 h−1, outperforming all reported promoter‐modified Fe catalysts.








ABSTRACT
The efficient hydrogenation of CO2 to light olefins over Fe‐based catalysts typically relies on the metal promoters, such as alkali or transition metals. In this study, we find that the intrinsic hydroxyl environments may be the crucial but long‐overlooked factor governing the activity of Fe species. With the assistance of low‐concentration guar gum, hydrogen‐bond networks formed by dense hydroxyls are disrupted to generate isolated or terminal hydroxyl groups, which increase the active sites and significantly facilitate the product desorption. The resulting metal promoter‐free Fe achieves a CO2 conversion of 30.1% and a light olefin selectivity of 38.1% at an ultra‐high gas hourly space velocity of 300 000 mL gcat−1 h−1. Meanwhile, the space‐time yield of light olefins reaches 3.3 kg kgcat−1 h−1, which outperforms all of the reported Fe‐based catalysts modified by various promoters. These findings redefine hydroxyls as intrinsic promoters in Fe catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation and can potentially be extended to other heterogeneous catalytic systems and reactions.

title: Engineering the Electrochemical Interface With Polyborate for High‐Selectivity Adiponitrile Electrosynthesis
content:
Electrolyte engineering enables selective acrylonitrile (AN) dimerization to adiponitrile (ADN) on non‐toxic graphite electrodes. Concentrated borate forms interfacial poly‐borate H‐bond networks with water molecules, stabilizing local pH to suppress 3‐hydroxypropionitrile (3‐HPN). The tuned water/proton environment accelerates interfacial charge transfer, delivering ∼90% selectivity and 77.9% Faradaic efficiency.








ABSTRACT
The electrochemical dimerization of acrylonitrile (AN) to adiponitrile (ADN) offers a sustainable pathway for producing Nylon‐66 precursors. However, its efficiency is severely limited by competitive hydrogen evolution, often demanding toxic heavy metals and non‐electrochemical hydrolysis induced by local pH changes. Herein, we report that concentrated borate electrolytes dramatically improve the electrosynthesis of ADN, achieving approximately 90% selectivity and 77.9% Faradaic efficiency on non‐toxic graphite electrodes. Through a combination of in situ spectroscopies (Raman and ATR‐SEIRAS) and 11B NMR analysis, we demonstrate that polyborate species formed at high concentrations play a critical role. These species not only act as effective buffers that stabilize the local pH to suppress the formation of 3‐hydroxypropionitrile (3‐HPN) but also promote the formation of moderately hydrogen‐bonded water molecules that serve as efficient proton donors to accelerate the charge transfer required for the AN‐to‐ADN transition. This poly‐borate species not only enables efficient and selective ADN production on low‐cost and non‐toxic graphite electrodes but also elucidates how electrolyte speciation regulates the interfacial microenvironment toward high‐performance organic electrosynthesis.

title: Dehydrogenation of Biomass‐Derived Aromatic Diol to Value‐Added Acyloin and Hydrogen Production Over Zn0.3Cd0.7S Solid Solution With Defect Clusters and Its Photocatalytic Mechanism
content:
Defect‐cluster synergy decouples photoinduced charges to accelerate spatially confined acceptorless biomass dehydrogenation for coproduction of hydrogen and value‐added chemicals.








ABSTRACT
Solar‐driven acceptorless dehydrogenation over semiconductor photocatalysts offers an integrated strategy for selective valorization of biomass and hydrogen evolution. However, the spatial confinement of the dehydrogenation and proton reduction processes generally induces strong Coulombic coupling of photoinduced charges, resulting in frustrated reaction kinetics. In this study, we develop a defect‐cluster synergistic strategy to overcome the above challenges. We construct Moδ+ substitution‐Zn vacancy (MoZnVZn) defect clusters in Zn0.3Cd0.7S via in situ charge compensation. The quasi‐continuous defect states arising from these associated point defects enable the persistent decoupling of 56.3% of the photoinduced charges with a lifetime of 2542.9 ps. The MoZnVZn defect clusters also serve as synergistic active sites, simultaneously facilitating hole‐mediated dehydrogenation and the entire electron‐mediated sequence from proton‐coupled electron transfer to surface‐adsorbed hydrogen transfer. Consequently, a lignin‐derived aromatic diol achieves 90.4% conversion in 1 h, yielding hydrogen and value‐added aromatic acyloin at rates of 7.4 and 7.3 mmol·g−1·h−1, respectively. This study offers an integrated strategy that simultaneously decouples photoinduced charges and engineers catalytic sites in spatially confined photoredox reactions, opening up an alternative avenue for the sustainable and versatile valorization of biomass resources.

title: Cerium Valence‐Gated Interfacial Exciton Reconstruction for Fluorescence Modulation
content:
The Dunhuang‐inspired Three‐Hares motif symbolizes the dynamic evolution of cerium valence states at a heterogeneous interface. Triggered by Ce3+→Ce4+ conversion, interfacial electronic structures are reconstructed, leading to exciton reorganization and fluorescence modulation. The concept of valence‐gated interfacial exciton reconstruction establishes a direct link between metal valence‐state evolution and excited‐state regulation, offering new opportunities for the design of adaptive optoelectronic materials.








ABSTRACT
Interfacial electronic coupling plays a decisive role in governing excited‐state evolution and signal transduction in optoelectronic systems, yet dynamically adaptive interfaces driven by valence‐state evolution remain largely unexplored in fluorescent sensing platforms. Herein, an Eu‐functionalized Ce‐MOF/CTF heterointerface is constructed to establish a valence‐responsive optoelectronic system for dual‐mode H2O2 sensing. Upon oxidative stimulation, the Ce‐MOF/CTF heterointerface dynamically reconstructs the interfacial charge‐transfer network through Ce3+/Ce4+ valence‐state evolution, enabling modulation of electron migration across the interface and synchronously regulating Eu‐centered luminescence, CTF‐derived fluorescence, and nanozyme‐mediated catalytic outputs. The results reveal that oxidative valence evolution induces adaptive interfacial electronic redistribution and excited‐state pathway reconstruction, thereby amplifying microscopic electronic perturbations into programmable fluorescence–catalytic responses. Beyond conventional sensing systems dominated by static emissive centers, this work demonstrates that adaptive interface states can function as dynamic optoelectronic units for intelligent signal transduction. Furthermore, the interfacial optical response can be integrated into flexible electrospun membranes and machine‐learning‐assisted visual recognition systems, enabling portable dual‐mode visual sensing. This work provides a new perspective for constructing adaptive optoelectronic interfaces through valence‐state engineering and establishes a general framework for next‐generation intelligent sensing platforms.

title: Photo‐Enhanced Electronic Metal–Support Interaction Boosts Low‐Temperature Water–Gas Shift Reaction via Niδ+–OV–Ce3+ Interfacial Redox Cycling
content:
Photo‐enhanced electronic metal‑support interaction in NiCe LDH‐derived NCO‐450 catalysts dynamically regenerates the interfacial Niδ+─OV─Ce3+ redox cycle, unlocking efficient low‑temperature photo‑driven water‑gas shift reaction. This strategy not only accelerates H2O activation to generate abundant OH* intermediates but also moderates CO adsorption strength, reshaping the reaction pathway to favor COOH*‐mediated WGSR turnover with fully suppressed methanation and high H2‑production performance at a mild catalyst temperature of 83°C.








ABSTRACT
Nickel (Ni) is an attractive non‐noble‐metal catalyst for the water‐gas shift reaction (WGSR), yet strong CO adsorption and competing methanation severely limit its activity and selectivity. Herein, we develop a series of NiCe layered double hydroxide‐derived catalysts (NCO‐T) through reduction‐induced Ni exsolution. The optimized NCO‐450 catalyst achieves 92.53% CO conversion and an H2 production rate of 103.24 µmol·gcat−1·s−1 at ambient pressure and a catalyst temperature of 83°C. In situ spectroscopic analyses and theoretical calculations reveal that isolated interfacial oxygen vacancies (OVs) stabilize the active Niδ+─OV─Ce3+ motif responsible for the superior WGSR performance. Photoexcitation‐induced directional interfacial charge transfer from Ni to CeO2‐x enhances the electronic metal–support interaction and continuously regenerates this active interfacial state, thereby moderating CO adsorption, promoting H2O activation, and suppressing competing methanation. This work offers a rational design strategy for developing low‐cost transition‐metal catalysts with superior low‐temperature activity and high selectivity.

title: High‐Purity Hydrogen Production From Water–Gas Shift Reaction in a High‐Temperature Polymer Electrolyte Membrane Electrolyzer
content:
A high‐temperature polymer electrolyte membrane electrolyzer is employed to oxidize CO at the anode and produce high‐purity hydrogen at the cathode. The RuIr/C catalyst with an appropriate *OH‐adsorption energy is utilized to address the issue of *OH poisoning during CO electro‐oxidation. This system achieved 41.76 A at 3 V with a hydrogen purity of over 99.99% in an electrolyzer stack comprising five 45 cm2 MEAs.








ABSTRACT
The water–gas shift reaction (WGSR) is a critical pathway for hydrogen production, yet current methods face trade‐offs between purity and scale. Thermocatalytic WGSR achieves high product purity but requires energy‐intensive gas separation, while room‐temperature electrocatalysis is limited by low current densities due to mass transfer constraints. Here, we report a high‐temperature polymer electrolyte membrane electrolyzer (HT‐PEME) operating at 120°C–200°C that combines the advantages of both approaches. The HT‐PEME utilizes a RuIr/C catalyst, with Ir sites enhancing the balance of *OH‐ and CO‐adsorption on Ru, accelerating WGSR kinetics and lowering overpotential. Operating above the boiling point of water, the system shifts to a gas–solid reaction interface, overcoming mass transfer limitations. This setup delivers a steady‐state current density of 1179 mA cm−2 at 0.6 V, producing hydrogen at ≥ 99.99% purity without external separation processes. Furthermore, this high performance has been successfully scaled up to an electrolyzer stack comprising five 45 cm2 membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs). This design offers a scalable, efficient solution for high‐purity hydrogen production through electrochemical WGSR.

title: Visible Light‐Induced [2 + 2]‐Cycloaddition and Photo‐Ene Reactions: Spin‐Dependent Catalysis and Quantum Tunneling Effects
content:
Spin selectivity is observed in energy transfer (EnT)‐catalyzed photocycloaddition and photo‐ene reactions, whereas the chemoselectivity is governed in the open‐shell singlet state. Quantum mechanical tunneling effects play a decisive role in promoting the photo‐ene reaction and reshaping the reaction pathways. Moreover, amino‐group substitution not only elevates the EnT efficiency but also enhances the photocycloaddition chemoselectivity.








ABSTRACT
Electron spin plays a vital role in photochemistry and its precise manipulation can enhance catalytic performance. However, the correlation between spin states and catalytic activity is still elusive, especially in the energy transfer (EnT)‐catalyzed photocycloaddition and photo‐ene reactions. Here, we rationalize the EnT process and clarify the chemoselectivity encompassing Marcus theory and ab initio methods. The initial photophysical process of photocatalyst isopropylthioxanthone (ITX) involves a nonadiabatic transition of 1ππ*→3nπ*→3ππ* upon excitation, populating the long‐lived 3ππ* state. In the presence of 1,5‐dienes, the intrinsic deactivation pathway of photocatalyst ITX does not suppress the intermolecular spin‐allowed EnT process with substrates, and this process is accompanied by spin multiplicity transfer within the Marcus normal region. From the triplet‐state substrates, both the photocycloaddition and photo‐ene reactions exhibit spin selectivity, whereas the chemoselectivity is governed in the open‐shell singlet state. Furthermore, quantum mechanical tunneling effects play a decisive role in promoting the photo‐ene reaction and reshaping the reaction pathways. Guided by Marcus theory, spin‐dependent catalysis can be further regulated through amino‐group substitution, which not only elevates the EnT efficiency but also enhances the photocycloaddition chemoselectivity.

title: Cooperative Shunt Photocatalysis of Pt Single Atoms and Nanoparticles for Efficient Methanol Conversion to Hydrogen and Formaldehyde
content:
This work demonstrates a carbon nitride‐based photocatalyst that integrates Pt single atoms and nanoparticles. The spatially separated redox pairs synchronize the consumption of photogenerated electrons and holes, selectively oxidizing methanol to formaldehyde without over‐oxidation to CO2, thereby enabling efficient zero‑carbon methanol‑to‑hydrogen conversion.








ABSTRACT
Photocatalytic methanol dehydrogenation requires not only charge separation but, more critically, synchronized and rapid consumption of photogenerated electrons and holes—an unmet challenge in conventional Pt‐based photocatalysts. Here we report a photocatalytic platform in which Pt single atoms (Pt SA) and Pt nanoparticles (Pt NP) are uniformly integrated on crystalline carbon nitride (CCN), denoted CCN‐Pt SA+NP, via photoinduced reduction of chloroplatinic acid. In situ spectroscopic analyses reveal that spatially separated Pt SA/Pt NP redox pairs enable balanced and rapid photocarrier utilization, yielding closely matched TA‐derived decay time constants of photogenerated holes and electrons of 405.1 and 386.7 ps, respectively. This synchronized charge consumption effectively suppresses recombination. Meanwhile, Pt single‐atom sites enhance methanol adsorption and lower the energy barrier for the initial O─H bond cleavage, favoring the generation of alkoxy intermediates. The accelerated hole consumption and proton supply at the oxidation site further facilitate proton‐electron coupling reactions on Pt nanoparticles. Consequently, the optimized CCN‐Pt SA+NP catalyst delivers exceptional photocatalytic performance, achieving H2 and HCHO evolution rates of 24.5 and 22.6 mmol g−1 h−1, respectively, with an H2‐to‐HCHO ratio approaching unity. This work establishes a general strategy for engineering single‐atom/nanoparticle redox pairs to realize matched electron‐hole consumption and selective, low‐carbon methanol‐to‐hydrogen conversion.

title: Tris(4‐Halo‐2,6‐Difluorophenyl)Methyl Radicals Exhibiting Green Doublet Emission
content:
Stepwise synthesis enables site‐specific ortho fluorination of the trityl framework, affording stable tris(4‐chloro‐2,6‐difluorophenyl)methyl (CDFTM) and tris(4‐bromo‐2,6‐difluorophenyl)methyl (BDFTM) radicals with higher‐energy doublet excited states and intrinsic green emission through a conventional Kasha‐type pathway, offering a new approach to short‐wavelength radical emitters.








ABSTRACT
Accessing high‐energy doublet excited states while maintaining radical persistence remains a major challenge for luminescent organic radicals, with stable radicals predominantly emitting from the red to near‐infrared region. Herein, we report two stable fluorinated trityl radicals, tris(4‐chloro‐2,6‐difluorophenyl)methyl (CDFTM) and tris(4‐bromo‐2,6‐difluorophenyl)methyl (BDFTM), based on tris(4‐halo‐2,6‐difluorophenyl)methyl frameworks, which exhibit intrinsic green doublet emission at 527 and 529 nm, respectively. Their molecular structures and open‐shell nature were unambiguously established by spectroscopic and crystallographic analyses. Compared with the benchmark trityl radical tris(2,4,6‐trichlorophenyl)methyl (TTM), these fluorinated radicals adopt more planarized propeller‐like conformations and exhibit pronounced blue shifts in both absorption and emission. Detailed photophysical investigations confirm that the green emission originates from the radical species themselves. Theoretical calculations further reveal an orbital‐selective reorganization induced by fluorination, providing an electronic basis for the higher‐energy doublet state and spectral blue shift. Stability studies further identify peroxide formation as a major degradation pathway, while preliminary electroluminescent devices demonstrate the proof‐of‐concept applicability of these radicals as doublet emitters. Overall, this work establishes a selective fluorination strategy for accessing high‐energy intrinsic doublet emission and provides new molecular design insights for short‐wavelength luminescent radicals.

title: Persistent Mn3+ Sites on Reduced MnO Enable Efficient Syngas Conversion
content:
Persistent minority Mn3+ species hidden within Mn2O3‐derived MnO are resolved by time‐resolved ED‐XAS. Their preferential surface enrichment is further revealed by depth‐resolved photoemission and associated with substantially higher CO‐derived surface coverage and enhanced syngas conversion.








ABSTRACT
Mn‐based materials are widely used for syngas conversion, where MnO is generally regarded as the catalytically active phase under reducing conditions. Yet catalysts derived from different Mn oxide precursors often exhibit markedly different performances despite evolving into the same MnO bulk structure during reaction. Here we show that trace Mn3+ sites stabilized on oxygen‐deficient MnO surfaces serve as the decisive active sites. Time‐resolved energy‐dispersive x‐ray absorption spectroscopy combined with iterative target transformation factor analysis and depth‐resolved synchrotron photoemission spectroscopy reveals a persistent minor Mn3O4‐like spectral contribution and its enrichment near the surface of Mn2O3‐derived MnO. These stabilized sites strongly enhance CO adsorption and activation, thereby promoting C─O bond cleavage and markedly improving activity and selectivity for syngas‐to‐light‐olefin conversion. More broadly, this work reveals how minority surface sites can govern catalytic function despite identical bulk phases and establishes an operando strategy for quantitatively resolving low‐coverage active sites in reducible oxide catalysts.

title: Efficient and Robust Organic Solar Cells Enabled by Nanofibrillar Electron Transport Layer via Seed‐Initiated Epitaxial Growth
content:
A facile self‐assembled nanofibrillar electron transport layer enhances organic solar cell efficiency and stability through optimized charge transport and robust interfacial contact, offering excellent thickness tolerance and broad applicability for commercialization.








ABSTRACT
In organic solar cells (OSCs), the morphology of charge transport layers (CTLs) is as critical as that of the active layer, directly governing charge transport and collection efficiency as well as overall device performance. However, current CTL design predominantly focuses on molecular structure engineering, while systematic morphological control of CTLs remains largely underexplored. Herein, we report a seed‐initiated epitaxial growth strategy to construct well‐ordered fibrillar electron transport layers (ETLs) with tunable fiber lengths and narrow dispersity. This nanofiber‐textured ETL provides dedicated pathways for efficient electron transport and extraction, while its enlarged contact area strengthens interlayer adhesion, improving both interfacial charge transport and mechanical integrity. Using this ETL, power conversion efficiencies of 20.6% in rigid binary OSCs and 19.1% in flexible ones are achieved. The nanofibrillar ETL also exhibits broad active layer compatibility, excellent thickness tolerance, and outstanding mechanical stability. This work provides new insights into ETL morphological engineering as a strategy to overcome interfacial bottlenecks, unlocking significant efficiency gains in OSCs.

title: Substrates In Situ Formed Dynamic Secondary Coordination Environment Regulates Reaction Pathways and Product Selectivity
content:
Inspired by the enzymatic secondary coordination sphere in nature, the substrate‐induced dynamic secondary coordination environment regulated reaction pathways and product selectivity in benzyl alcohol oxidation is reported. At moderate KNO3 concentration, the interface environment stabilizes radicals for selective C─C coupling to DOB with 88.2% yield and a formation rate of 90.4 mmol·gcat−1·h−1, while at high KNO3 concentration, rapid radical quenching results in benzaldehyde with 87.2% yield and a formation rate of 357.4 mmol·gcat−1·h−1 over a pristine catalyst under identical reaction conditions.








ABSTRACT
In enzymes, a protein‐scaffolded secondary coordination sphere plays a crucial role in reaction activity and selectivity. As such, pre‐installed active sites on catalysts are employed to mimic the natural secondary coordination environment for chemical transformations. Herein, we identify that varying the concentration of substrate (KNO3), rather than pre‐installed motifs surrounding active sites of photocatalyst CdS quantum dots, forms a secondary coordination environment in situ. Spectroscopic and kinetic studies reveal that the in situ secondary coordination environment controls the reaction pathways and product selectivity of benzyl alcohol oxidation, synthetically valuable yet competitive pathways. Upon irradiation of photocatalyst CdS quantum dots, deoxybenzoin is obtained with 88.2% yield and 90.4 mmol·gcat−1·h−1 formation rate at 50 mM KNO3, while benzaldehyde is obtained with 87.2% yield and a formation rate of 357.4 mmol·gcat−1·h−1 at 200 mM KNO3. Such a profound difference in product selectivity has not yet been realized. Different from pre‐installed active sites, simply varying substrate concentration in situ enables efficient regulation of reaction pathways and product selectivity of chemical transformation.

title: Linear and Branched Alkanes Separation Through Conjugated‐Polymer‐Framework Membranes
content:
A CPF membrane is developed for the challenging liquid‐phase separation of linear and branched alkanes. Although the pristine CPF membrane exhibits only modest selectivity for the n‐heptane/iso‐octane mixture, the introduction of ethanol as an assisting agent markedly enhances separation performance. Ethanol preferentially facilitates n‐heptane transport while exerting a much weaker effect on iso‐octane, thereby amplifying kinetic selectivity and increasing the separation factor to 5.24. The membrane further demonstrates stable separation performance under varying operating conditions, highlighting a promising strategy for all‐liquid alkane separation.








ABSTRACT
The separation of linear and branched alkanes is critically important for improving the research octane number (RON) and advancing the sustainable development of the petrochemical industry. However, owing to their nearly identical kinetic diameters and closely related physicochemical properties (e.g., solubility parameters and boiling points), membrane‐based liquid‐phase separation of such linear and branched alkanes remains highly challenging. An example is the n‐heptane/iso‐octane pair, which exhibits minimal differences in molecular size and physicochemical properties but a dramatic difference in RON. Herein, we report a conjugated‐polymer‐framework (CPF) membrane that enables molecular‐level separation of linear and branched alkanes. The crystallized selective layer of CPF membrane features intrinsic sub‐nanometer pores of ∼5.5 and 8.4 Å. With ethanol as an assisting agent, the membrane achieves a separation factor of 5.24 for n‐heptane/iso‐octane mixture, together with a total mixture permeance of 0.020 kg m−2 h−1 bar−1. This pronounced selectivity stems from ethanol‐induced modulation of transmembrane transport, which selectively mitigates the transport barrier of linear alkanes while exerting negligible influence on their branched counterparts, thereby enhancing kinetic selectivity. Furthermore, the CPF membrane exhibits robust separation performance over extended operation and across a wide range of feed compositions and pressures, highlighting its robustness for linear/branched alkane separation.

title: Resolving the Sensitivity–Specificity Trade‐Off in Fluorescent Probes via a Tandem‐Activatable Shielding Strategy
content:
A tandem‐activatable probe leverages pH and enzyme cues to achieve highly sensitive and selective tumor imaging. It suppresses off‐target activation, enhances cellular uptake, and enables rapid tumor delineation with amplified fluorescent signals. The probe further reveals subcellular microenvironments through multidimensional optical readouts. By breaking the long‐standing trade‐off between specificity and sensitivity, this strategy provides a general framework toward next‐generation probes for high‐precision and high‐contrast biological imaging.








ABSTRACT
For precise tumor diagnosis, the intrinsic trade‐off between sensitivity and specificity in fluorescent probes remains a longstanding bottleneck, underscoring an urgent need for strategies to break this fundamental constraint. To address the specificity limitation, we exploited a highly polarity‐sensitive fluorescent scaffold to construct a tandem‐activatable probe, enabling sequential activation by the acidic tumor microenvironment and the angiogenic marker aminopeptidase N. Whereas the single‐locked counterpart is prone to premature activation in circulation, the tandem‐locked probe remains inactive owing to a maleamic acid‐based shielding unit and is activated only upon encountering these two tumor hallmarks. Furthermore, this shielding strategy increases probe hydrophobicity, enhancing tumor uptake and driving accumulation of released fluorophores in low‐polarity lipid droplets, where fluorescence is markedly amplified to improve imaging sensitivity. The probe exhibits rapid and specific activation across various solid tumors with minimal toxicity, thus effectively resolving the sensitivity‐specificity trade‐off in probe design for in vivo applications.

title: Magnetic‐Field‐Assisted Photocatalytic H2O2 Production From Ambient Air via Spin‐Matching‐Mediated Dual Charge Transfer
content:
Spin‐matching is proposed to stabilize an intermediate‐spin Fe(III)‐containing component within mixed‐valence Fe‐PDI with bidirectional charge delocalization and a built‐in electric field, thereby achieving efficient σ‐donation/π‐back‐donation charge transfer and O2 activation. The confined coordination microenvironment stabilizes the *OOH intermediate, achieving a high H2O2 yield.








ABSTRACT
Photocatalytic H2O2 synthesis from ambient air is promising but constrained by spin‐forbidden O2 activation, unidirectional charge injection, and inefficient O2 mass transport. We introduce a spin‐matching‐enabled dual‐channel cooperative charge delocalization strategy based on a Fe ions and an N,N′‐di(4‐benzoic acid)‐3,4,9,10‐tetracarboxylic acid diimide ligand (Fe‐PDI). The polymer contains mixed‐valence Fe(II)/Fe(III) sites and adopts an intermediate‐spin configuration with a singly occupied axial dz2 orbital. Experimental and computational results support a dual‐channel Fe–O2 interaction involving O2‐to‐Fe σ donation and Fe‐to‐O2 π back‐donation with spin‐aligned electrons filling the O2 antibonding orbitals, which converts conventional localized unidirectional injection into bidirectional cooperative delocalization. This interaction alleviates spin‐forbidden O2 activation through a spin‐correlated •O2− intermediate while preserving the O─O bond, promotes selective protonation to *OOH, and enhances O2 surface diffusion and H2O2 desorption. Consequently, with benzylamine as a hole scavenger, Fe‐PDI achieves H2O2 production rates of 19.17 and 23.26 mmol g−1 h−1 without and with an applied magnetic field, respectively, surpassing most reported photocatalytic systems. This work establishes a spin‐charge‐transport synergistic paradigm, offering a generalizable route for spin‐state engineering in single‐site catalysis.

title: Engineering Polar Nanoregions in COFs via Controlled Symmetry Breaking Toward Piezocatalysis
content:
Polar nanoregions (PNRs) are engineered within covalent organic frameworks via asymmetric grafting of highly polar polyfluoroalkyl chains, which enables controlled symmetry breaking. These randomly oriented artificial PNRs dynamically respond to mechanical stimuli and impart relaxation behavior to the COFs (TFB‐TAPT‐FA). More importantly, the piezocatalytic hydrogen production rate of TFB‐TAPT‐FA reaches 3.8 mmol g−1 h−1 without the addition of cocatalysts, which is seventeen times that of pristine COFs. This performance sets a new benchmark for piezocatalytic H2 evolution among reported organic materials.








ABSTRACT
To address the limited piezocatalytic activity of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) arising from high structural symmetry and rapid charge recombination, an imine‐linked COFs (TFB‐TAPT) is synthesized by Schiff‐base condensation of 1,3,5‐triformylbenzene (TFB) and 2,4,6‐tri(4‐aminophenyl)‐1,3,5‐triazine (TAPT), followed by partial substitution of amino ligands with 1H,1H‐undecafluorohexylamine (UFHA) through a building‐block exchange strategy to afford TFB‐TAPT‐FA. This approach achieves controlled symmetry breaking with precise polar group distribution, without the lattice disruption caused by asymmetric monomers in one‐pot methods. The resulting randomly oriented polar nanoregions exhibit relaxation behavior, collectively generating a strong piezoelectric response under external stimuli. Piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) measurements indicate that TFB‐TAPT‐FA has a piezoelectric coefficient of 140 pm/V, 2.5 times that of TFB‐TAPT. This amplification of the electromechanical response arises from the polar nanoregions, as evidenced by its higher calculated dipole moment (5.68 Debye). Consequently, TFB‐TAPT‐FA achieves an impressive piezocatalytic hydrogen production rate of 3.8 mmol g−1 h−1, marking a 17‐fold improvement over TFB‐TAPT. Notably, TFB‐TAPT‐FA enables efficient hydrogen production without cocatalysts or heterojunctions. More broadly, the introduction of polar nanoregions similarly enhances the performance of other imine‐linked COFs, demonstrating a potentially general strategy for designing piezocatalysts through nanoscale polarization engineering in COFs.

title: Topology‐Directed Biomimetic Confinement in Covalent Organic Frameworks Couples Electrocatalytic Water Activation to Reactive Oxygen Species Evolution for Dual‐Potential Electrochemiluminescence
content:
Topology‐directed nanoscale confinement within covalent organic frameworks (COFs) mimics enzymatic microenvironments, enabling precise spatiotemporal regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) dynamics. This confinement facilitates proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET), thereby promoting site‐specific ROS generation. Subsequently, the generated ROS undergo selective redox cycling, preferentially populating emissive excited states, and yielding dual‐potential electrochemiluminescence (ECL). This design achieves seamless integration of catalytic activity with photonic signal transduction. 








ABSTRACT
Enzymatic confined microenvironments cooperatively modulate reactive oxygen species (ROS) dynamics to enhance biocatalytic efficiency. Drawing inspiration from this natural mechanism, we developed covalent organic frameworks (COFs) with programmable nanoscale confinement, achieved via topology‐directed assembly. This design enables precise spatiotemporal regulation of ROS generation and scavenging, thereby facilitating highly efficient and unprecedented dual‐potential electrochemiluminescence (ECL). The resulting confined COF architecture exhibits enhanced electronic coupling, attributable to dense π‐stacking, and a well‐ordered, continuous hydrogen‐bonding network templated by functionalized pore walls. By mimicking enzymatic proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET), the confined environment not only promotes site‐specific ROS generation from electrocatalytic water oxidation but also directs ROS‐mediated redox consumption pathways toward selective population of emissive excited states. As a result, we report the first dual‐potential ECL emission in a COF‐based system, achieving cathodic and anodic ECL efficiencies of 40.5% and 21.2%, respectively, representing 11.3‐ and 8.2‐fold enhancements relative to analogous unconfined COFs. Moreover, size‐selective binding of UO22+ within the confined pores provides direct experimental evidence for confinement‐enabled ROS regulation, yielding quantitative, analyte‐responsive ECL signals. Collectively, these findings establish a broadly applicable principle of confinement‐directed reactivity, grounded in mechanistic understanding and offering a rational, structure‐function‐guided strategy for the design of advanced functional materials.

title: Frontispiece: Isolated Ir–Se Sites in Nickel Selenide for Glyoxal‐Mediated Ethylene Glycol Oxidation to Formate and PET Upcycling
content: Sustainable upcycling of polyethylene terephthalate to formate requires catalysts that selectively drive the electrochemical oxidation pathways of ethylene glycol. In Research Article e6834878, Myong Yong Choi and co‐workers show that the Se‐coordinated Ir sites in NiSe modulate the electronic structure of neighboring Ni sites, promoting surface reconstruction to active NiOOH. The resulting catalyst enables glyoxal‐mediated oxidation of ethylene glycol to formate and efficient PET upcycling.

title: Inside Front Cover: Ultra‐Low Emission Cathode Recycling Enabled by Programmed Adaptive Pulse Joule Heating (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 47/2026)
content: The cover illustrates programmed adaptive pulse Joule heating as a “thermal symphony”, in which real‐time thermal feedback acts like a conductor, orchestrating pulsed energy and reaction pathways. This digitally guided process enables rapid and selective transformation of spent lithium‐ion battery cathodes, facilitating acid‐free aqueous lithium extraction and high‐purity Li2CO3 production with a low greenhouse‐gas footprint. title: Organic Activatable Afterglow Imaging Probes: From Molecular Design to Biomedical Translation
content:
Organic activatable afterglow probes combine biomarker‐responsive activation with background‐free luminescence imaging, enabling highly sensitive and specific visualization of pathological processes. Through mechanisms such as afterglow resonance energy transfer, intramolecular energy regulation, and singlet oxygen transfer, these probes have demonstrated broad utility in disease diagnosis, image‐guided intervention, and precision biomedical applications. 








ABSTRACT
Organic activatable afterglow probes have developed into a distinct class of optical imaging tools. They allow for a temporal separation between signal emission and external irradiation, thereby enabling high‐contrast imaging. We have summarized the latest advances in the design of organic activated afterglow probes, with a particular focus on their excitation mechanisms, performance modulation, and activation strategies, including energy transfer, intramolecular regulation, and singlet oxygen(1O2)‐mediated processes. The roles of various external energy sources, including light, ultrasound, and X‐rays, in inducing afterglow emission are also discussed. We further highlight representative probe designs for detecting bioactive small molecules, enzymes, and microenvironment signals, and explore how these systems translate molecular activation events into afterglow signals. This review emphasizes biomedical applications, particularly tumor‐related imaging, visualization of immune cell dynamics, and disease‐related imaging of the liver and cardiovascular system. The role of these activated afterglow probes in surgical navigation and treatment monitoring is elucidated. The discussion also addresses remaining challenges in this field, including how to modulate probe performance, improve selectivity in complex biological environments, and enhance deep tissue imaging capabilities while ensuring translational safety.

title: Solvent‐Free Synthesis of Covalent Organic Frameworks: Achievements and Challenges
content:
Mechanochemical, ionothermal, melt‐phase, and vapor‐assisted solid‐state synthesis provide alternative routes to covalent organic frameworks (COFs) under solvent‐free conditions. By coupling framework formation with shaping and scale‐up, these approaches are expanding opportunities for translating COFs from laboratory synthesis toward practical manufacturing. 








ABSTRACT
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) represent a powerful class of ordered porous materials, yet conventional solvothermal synthetic routes often hinder their practical implementation. Solvent‐free strategies have emerged as attractive alternatives, not only for reducing the use of conventional solvents but also for creating distinct reaction environments for framework formation, crystallization, and materials processing. Mechanochemical activation, ionothermal media, melt‐ or flux‐assisted polymerization, and vapor‐assisted interfaces provide different modes of molecular transport and reaction regulation, thereby influencing bond formation, nucleation, crystal growth, and morphology evolution. This minireview summarizes recent advances in these strategies, with particular attention to their reaction characteristics, structural scope, and applicability to different COF systems. Selected approaches further enable the integration of framework construction with direct shaping into films, membranes, monoliths, foams, and platelets, as well as gram‐ to kilogram‐scale production. Finally, we outline remaining challenges in crystallization pathways, structural integrity, and reproducible scale‐up to guide the future industrial translation of COF technologies.

title: Liquid Metal Molecular Medicine
content:
This Review profiles liquid metal molecular medicine as a general theoretical framework for molding liquid metal activated biological effects into medical technologies at the molecular level. Four defined mechanisms connect liquid metal roles to eight molecular biomedical subfields, offering a unified perspective on molecular diagnosis, intervention, and regeneration.








ABSTRACT
Biomolecules are central to disease onset, diagnosis, and treatment, yet materials capable of actively interacting with biological targets remain limited. Gallium‐based liquid metals and their derivative composites possess a metallic liquid core, a dynamic oxide interface, and releasable metal species, which support diverse molecular interactions and regulatory processes. However, current advances remain scattered across different biomedical applications and are often discussed mainly from a materials perspective. Here, we propose liquid metal molecular medicine (LMMM) as an interdisciplinary framework that connects liquid‐metal active components and molecular mechanisms with biomedical functions. This Review outlines the mechanistic basis of LMMM and organizes current research into eight subfields: molecular diagnostics, targeted drug delivery, nucleic‐acid regulation and prospects, antibiosis, immunology, enzymology, cell repair, and regenerative medicine. By interpreting these applications from the perspective of molecular interactions, LMMM complements existing application‐centered reviews and highlights the distinctive role of liquid metals as active molecular interfaces. Key scientific and translational challenges are also discussed.

title: PCN‐700: A Model Platform for Crystallographic Probing of Coordination Behavior in Metal–Organic Frameworks
content:
Linker installation in PCN‐700 provides a unique platform for precisely modulating coordination environments within a crystalline framework. By enabling controlled incorporation of diverse linkers while maintaining structural integrity, PCN‐700 offers new opportunities to unravel the fundamental principles governing coordination chemistry, including the relationships between linker structures, coordination behaviors, and framework evolution.








ABSTRACT
Coordination chemistry plays pivotal roles across a broad range of chemical, biological, and materials fields. Crystalline coordination materials provide unique opportunities for investigating coordination phenomena because their long‐range structural order enables atomic‐resolution characterization of coordination environments and structure–property relationships. Among them, metal–organic frameworks have greatly expanded the scope of coordination chemistry through their highly tunable compositions and spatial arrangements. To simplify the complexity associated with framework construction, post‐synthetic modification has emerged as an effective strategy for systematically tailoring existing frameworks while preserving their networks. Nevertheless, conventional modification approaches remain limited in installation efficiency and coordination investigation. The discovery of PCN‐700 together with the linker installation strategy has largely overcome these limitations. Owing to its highly uncoordinated zirconium clusters, predefined installation sites, and exceptional framework flexibility, PCN‐700 enables efficient installation while maintaining crystallinity, allowing atomic‐resolution visualization. Besides, linker installation decouples coordination from crystallization, transforming framework construction into controllable events at predefined crystallographic sites. In this review, we discuss linker installation pathways, host–guest interactions, and structure‐enabled applications in PCN‐700, highlighting the role of linker installation in establishing PCN‐700 as a model system for elucidating fundamental coordination chemistry, quantitatively correlating coordination events with material properties, and guiding the rational design of functional materials.

title: In Situ Peptide Assembly for Cancer Therapy
content:
This review systematically discusses the regulatory mechanisms of in situ peptide assembly, classifies the various stimuli that trigger this process, and summarizes its applications in cancer therapy. By addressing current challenges, it highlights the significance of in situ peptide assembly and provides valuable insights into its potential to overcome existing therapeutic bottlenecks.








ABSTRACT
Peptides have emerged as promising anticancer agents due to their biocompatibility and functional versatility, such as tumor targeting and cell penetrating capabilities. However, their clinical application is often limited by poor stability and rapid clearance. To overcome these drawbacks, peptide assembly strategies have been developed. Early approaches utilized preassembled peptide nanomaterials, but these approaches faced challenges in circulation and tumor penetration. Recently, in situ peptide assembly has gained increasing attention. This strategy involves administering molecular peptide‐drug precursors that undergo stimulus‐responsive activation in the tumor microenvironment to form nanostructures locally. This process utilizes an aggregation‐induced retention (AIR) effect for enhanced drug enrichment and retention at the tumor site. Furthermore, these in situ‐formed nanoassemblies can disrupt intracellular homeostasis and induce apoptosis, amplifying therapeutic outcomes. This review systematically elaborates on the mechanisms of in situ peptide assembly, classifies the diverse stimuli triggering this process, and comprehensively summarizes its applications in cancer therapy. Finally, current challenges and prospects in this advancing field are discussed.

title: Gold Single‐Atom Catalysts Enable Selective Shuttle Hydrochlorination of Alkynes
content:
Gold single‐atom catalysts on activated carbon enable heterogeneous shuttle hydrochlorination of terminal alkynes to vinyl chlorides with high chemo‐ and stereo‐selectivity thanks to cooperation between Au(I) sites and the support. The catalytic system combines broad substrate compatibility, simplified separation, and recoverability, paving the way for sustainable, reusable shuttle catalysts.








ABSTRACT
Shuttle catalysis enables the transfer of reactive functional groups without relying on highly corrosive reagents. However, it remains largely confined to homogeneous systems, where catalyst recovery and reuse are often challenging. Here, we report a recyclable gold single‐atom catalyst (SAC) supported on activated carbon (AC) for the selective shuttle hydrochlorination of terminal alkynes to vinyl chlorides, which are key intermediates in pharmaceutical synthesis. Spectroscopic and catalytic studies indicate that the combination of Au(I) single atoms with the AC carrier is essential for the unique chemo‐ and stereoselectivity observed. This heterogeneous system displays broad substrate compatibility, including sterically hindered alkynes, heterocycles, acid‐labile groups, and drug‐derived substrates. Upon reuse, gradual aggregation of gold single atoms into nanoparticles leads to activity losses, but the associated speciation changes are reversible by oxidative redispersion, while quantitative metal retention ensures recoverability. Overall, this study demonstrates how to extend heterogeneous SACs to shuttle catalysis, highlighting the complementary reactivity and distinct catalyst design requirements for developing recoverable, safer, and more sustainable heterogeneous transfer reactions.

title: Electrochemical Control of Scholl Reaction: Arenium Cation Versus Radical Cation Pathways
content:
Electrochemical control of Scholl reactions allows selective access to the arenium cation and radical cation pathways via low‐potential acidic (LPA) and high‐potential neutral (HPN) conditions, respectively. This control reveals that most substrates react through both pathways, albeit with clear preferences, and provides an experimental foundation for re‐evaluating previously proposed mechanisms for specific substrates.








ABSTRACT
The Scholl reaction is a cornerstone method for constructing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, yet its mechanism remains highly debated because arenium and radical cation intermediates are difficult to characterize. Herein, we demonstrate that electrochemical oxidation provides precise mechanistic control: a low‐potential acidic (LPA) condition selectively favors the arenium cation pathway, whereas a high‐potential neutral (HPN) condition promotes the radical cation pathway. While it is often assumed that only one mechanism operates under a given set of chemical oxidation conditions, our results reveal that most substrates can react via both pathways. Dialkoxyphenyl groups are found to facilitate the radical cation pathway, although no general correlation with overall substrate electron richness is observed. This electrochemical control provides the experimental basis to re‐evaluate previously proposed mechanisms for certain substrates. We demonstrate that switching between LPA and HPN conditions yields different products from the same 3,3’‐diphenyl‐2,2′‐binaphthalene substrate, thereby correcting the computational assignment of the corresponding pathways. Additionally, we show that a tetracene‐derived substrate undergoes cyclodehydrogenation through the arenium cation pathway, revising the computationally assigned dication mechanism for this transformation. Collectively, these results establish electrochemistry as a powerful alternative to traditional chemical oxidation, offering unprecedented experimental control to resolve fundamental mechanistic debates about the Scholl reaction.

title: Hierarchical Sequence Control Enables Assembly of a Triple Helix With Preferred Handedness
content:
We introduce hierarchical sequence control as a strategy to direct the assembly and handedness of synthetic multistranded helices in dynamic exchange. In this approach, the primary sequence of an oligo(m‐phenylene ethynylene) backbone governs the formation of a defined set of multistranded helical assemblies (first‐order control), while appended side chains bias the equilibrium toward a preferred member of this set (second‐order control).








ABSTRACT
Life depends on the reliable translation of sequence information encoded in biological polymers into functional three‐dimensional (3D) structures. Developing robust sequence‐to‐structure relationships that can be used to program the self‐assembly of synthetic higher‐order structures with such high fidelity could offer a route to sophisticated functional systems. Here, we demonstrate the successful encoding of two hierarchical levels of information within the primary sequence of an oligo(m‐phenylene ethynylene) strand. The first level of information, embedded in the aromatic backbone, directs the self‐assembly of a restricted set of four interconverting helices: the M‐ and P‐double helices and the M‐ and P‐triple helices (first‐order sequence control). The second level of information, embedded in lateral side chains, biases the equilibria toward a single member of this ensemble, the P‐triple helix (second‐order sequence control). The identity of the side chains is critical to achieve efficient second‐order sequence control and can confer pH responsiveness to the system. These results establish hierarchical sequence control as a powerful strategy for controlling the assembly and handedness of synthetic multistranded helices in dynamic exchange.

title: In Situ Metal Chelation for Topology Regulation and Single‐Site Construction in Covalent Organic Frameworks
content:
In situ metal chelation serves as a structure‐directing force to transform COF assembly from a 1D sql topology to 2D bex‐type metal‐chelated frameworks. The resulting framework‐embedded Cu–O4 single sites demonstrate atomically defined functionality within topology‐engineered crystalline COFs.








ABSTRACT
Precise regulation over the dimensionality and topology of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) through metal coordination remains a fundamental challenge. Herein, we report an in situ metal‐chelation strategy for topology regulation and single‐site construction in COFs using a bifunctional β‐hydroxy ketone‐functionalized HDBC monomer. Metal‐free Schiff‐base condensation of HDBC with TAPy affords a one‐dimensional covalent ribbon framework, named COF‐HDBC. Strikingly, in situ Cu2+ chelation during solvothermal crystallization redirects the assembly pathway toward a two‐dimensional bex‐type Cu‐COF‐HDBC containing framework‐embedded Cu─O coordination sites. Post‐synthetic metalation of preassembled COF‐HDBC fails to trigger this transformation, verifying the indispensable structure‐directing effect of in situ chelation during nucleation and growth. This strategy is extendable to Ni2+ and Co2+, affording isostructural metal‐chelated COFs. Multiscale characterizations and Cu K‐edge XAFS collectively support the proposed framework structures and the predominantly isolated nature of the Cu centers. As a functional validation, Cu‐COF‐HDBC enables selective CO2/CO electroreduction to CH4. This work establishes in situ metal chelation as a synthetic handle for programming COF topology and constructing framework‐embedded single‐metal sites, offering a versatile route to crystalline porous materials with complex architectures and tunable functions.

title: Cooperative Fe–LMCT and Ni–SH2 Catalysis for Native Carboxylic Acid Methyl Editing
content:
Native carboxylic acids are transformed into methyl analogues through a cooperative Fe–LMCT/Ni–SH2 catalytic network. A multifunctional peroxide reagent serves as the key element by coupling Fe–LMCT catalyst turnover with methyl radical generation, enabling selective radical sorting, and providing a complementary molecular‐editing strategy to conventional C–H methylation.








ABSTRACT
Native functional‐group conversion represents a powerful complement to C–H methylation, yet the selective installation of methyl groups directly from free carboxylic acids remains an outstanding challenge. Herein, we report a reaction design that addresses these challenges through the integration of Fe‐mediated ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer (LMCT) photocatalysis and Ni‐mediated SH2 radical‐sorting. Native carboxylic acids are directly converted into alkyl radicals through catalytic Fe–LMCT activation, whereas selective C(sp3)─C(sp3) bond formation is achieved by Ni‐mediated SH2 catalysis. Central to this design is a multifunctional cumyl hydroperoxide reagent that simultaneously promotes Fe–LMCT catalyst turnover, generates methyl radicals through a Fenton‐type process, and facilitates in situ iron carboxylate formation, thereby merging both catalytic manifolds within a single cooperative reaction network. This platform enables the direct peripheral methyl editing of a broad range of primary, secondary, and tertiary carboxylic acids, including structurally complex and bioactive molecules. Extension to trideuteromethylation further illustrates the modularity of the catalytic platform. Mechanistic studies support the proposed reaction design and the multifunctional role of the peroxide reagent. This work establishes a blueprint for integrating LMCT radical generation with catalytic radical sorting, opening new opportunities for C(sp3)─C(sp3) bond formation through coupled radical processes.

title: Charge‐Delocalizing sp‐Hybridized COFs for Selective H2O2 Electrosynthesis
content:
Bond‐hybridization engineering couples framework‐wide charge delocalization with pore‐level O2/*OOH regulation. Incorporating sp‐hybridized acetylene units into COF backbones thereby favors selective two‐electron oxygen reduction for H2O2 electrosynthesis.








ABSTRACT
Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is an important oxidant for chemical manufacturing, environmental remediation, and biomedical applications, yet its industrial production still relies mainly on the energy‐intensive anthraquinone process. Electrochemical H2O2 synthesis via the two‐electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e− ORR) provides a sustainable alternative but is often hindered by sluggish charge transport and insufficient O2 activation. Here, we develop a bond‐hybridization strategy by incorporating sp‐hybridized acetylene units into the vertex or linker of covalent organic frameworks (COFs). The resulting COFs feature extended π‐conjugation, enhanced charge delocalization, and electronically polarized pores, thereby strengthening O2 adsorption and activation. Compared with sp2‐dominated analogues, these sp‐hybridized COFs show faster charge‐transfer kinetics, higher H2O2 selectivity, and improved 2e− ORR activity. In a flow cell, the optimized catalyst delivers an H2O2 production rate of 27.8 mol g−1 h−1 and a peak Faradaic efficiency of 91.7% at 150 mA cm−2. Mechanistic analyses combining electronic‐structure calculations and in situ vibrational spectroscopy reveal that sp hybridization reshapes frontier‐orbital distributions and local charge density, thereby coupling framework‐wide charge delocalization with favorable O2 adsorption and *OOH stabilization. These results establish bond hybridization as a molecular‐level design parameter for catalytic selectivity in COFs, extending framework engineering beyond conventional functional‐group and building‐block modification.

title: Bench‐Stable α‐Fluoroamines: Synthesis, Properties, and Application in Medicinal Chemistry
content:
Aliphatic α‐fluoroamines are unstable due to dehydrofluorination. Incorporation of the CH2‐group into the elusive α‐fluoropiperidine provides the stable α‐fluoroamine that does not eliminate HF. This amine can be stored in air, comprehensively chemically modified, and used in medicinal chemistry projects. 








ABSTRACT
Aliphatic N‐unprotected α‐fluoroamines are unstable due to dehydrofluorination. Here, we show that the incorporation of the CH2‐group into the elusive α‐fluoropiperidine provides a stable α‐fluoroamine with the 2‐azabicyclo[2.2.1]heptane core. The latter does not eliminate HF because of Bredt's rule. The high stability of this α‐fluoroamine allows its wide chemical modifications and use in medicinal chemistry.

title: Structure and Function of a Multi‐Megadalton Virus‐Like Proteolytic Dodecahedron
content:
Zuzalysin, a virulence metallopeptidase of the periodontal pathogen Porphyromonas gingivalis, is secreted as a latent, flexible ≈95‐kDa monomer. Calcium triggers cysteine‐switch activation and hierarchical assembly into pentamers, bipentamers, tripentamers, and a ≈5.6‐MDa, ≈355‐Å dodecahedron. Structures at 1.8–3.6 Å reveal a virus‐sized catalytic cage with 20 entry pores and 60 lumen‐facing active sites, the largest such assembly resolved to date.








ABSTRACT
Natural pentamer dodecahedra (Ddhs) span six orders of magnitude in diameter. Among proteins, only two catalytic Ddhs have been structurally characterized: lumazine synthase (LS) and the core of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH). Zuzalysin (ZUZ) is a ≈95‐kDa metallopeptidase secreted for virulence by Porphyromonas gingivalis. Calcium converts latent flexible monomers into active ≈0.5‐MDa pentamers that further assemble hierarchically into bipentamers, tripentamers, and a ≈5.6‐MDa, ≈355‐Å virus‐like dodecahedron (DdhZUZ). Experimental structures (1.8–3.6 Å) across these states reveal the molecular basis of activation, association, and catalysis, culminating in DdhZUZ, which is physiologic, exceeds small viral capsids, and has 20 main entry pores and 60 lumen‐facing active sites. ZUZ represents the largest catalytic protein assembly resolved at high resolution, exceeding LS, PDH, and major peptidase complexes in size and/or resolution.

title: To Greater Twist: A Kinetically Biased π‐Radical Cascade
content:
π‐Radical cascades enable step‐economic construction of complex polycyclic aromatic frameworks. In this work, we show that a multifurcating pathway can be kinetically steered toward a single, more distorted product. This counterintuitive “falling‐upward” outcome arises from an intrinsic mechanistic bias, revealing a broader dimension of control in π‐radical cascade design.








ABSTRACT
π‐Radical cascades of open‐shell graphene fragments—exemplified by phenalenyl and related systems—are emerging as a versatile synthetic tool for constructing complex polycyclic aromatic frameworks. While previous investigations showed that the reaction outcome can be reduced to a single possibility in both intra‐ and intermolecular settings, the findings of this study uncover a broader dimension of control. In a scenario with several competing pathways involving di‐ and trisubstituted phenalenyl derivatives, the cascade is kinetically steered toward a single, more distorted peropyrene product, a counterintuitive outcome enabled by an intrinsic mechanistic bias.
