title: Defect Engineering via Aggregation: Unlocking Hour‐Long Afterglow and UV Thermoluminescence in Self‐Embedded Carbon Nitride Quantum Dots
content:
Self‐embedded carbon nitride quantum dots (CNQDs) exhibit aggregation‐induced energy‐storage luminescence through the synergistic effect of triplet stabilization and deep‐trap formation. The resulting system simultaneously achieves hour‐long afterglow, UV high‐temperature afterglow, and UV thermoluminescence for information encryption and time‐resolved imaging.








ABSTRACT
Carbon nitride quantum dots (CNQDs) exhibiting aggregation‐induced visible long persistent luminescence (LPL), ultraviolet (UV) high‐temperature afterglow (HTA), and thermoluminescence (TL) are reported for the first time. The CNQDs are synthesized via a facile solvent‐free thermolysis of biuret and display a blue LPL lasting over 1.5 h under ambient conditions. Upon heating to 150°C, intense UV HTA and TL emissions are generated. Mechanistic studies reveal that aggregation‐associated π–π stacking stabilizes triplet excitons, while aggregation‐stabilized defect‐related paramagnetic centers promote carrier capture and long‐term energy storage, with deeper traps serving as reservoirs for thermally activated release. Reverse intersystem crossing further transfers de‐trapped carriers from triplet to singlet excited states, resulting in a pronounced blue‐shift of the HTA and TL emissions into the UV region. Owing to the stability of the aggregates and their protective effect on excited states and trapped charges, the luminescence remains robust in aqueous dispersions, while the invisible UV TL signals remain clearly detectable after more than 15 days under ambient conditions. Leveraging these characteristics, we demonstrate applications in highly concealed information storage and high‐contrast bioimaging. This work establishes an aggregation‐induced defect‐engineering strategy for energy‐storage luminescent materials and opens a new pathway toward self‐embedded LPL/TL systems.

title: Mode‐Selective C═C and C─N Vibrational Coupling Modulates Nonradiative Decay in Regioisomeric Organic Phosphorescent Emission
content:
Regioisomerization redistributes local aromaticity and suppresses dominant C═C/C─N vibrational couplings, greatly inhibiting triplet nonradiative decay for enhanced organic room‐temperature phosphorescence. Mode‐resolved reorganization‐energy analysis unveils the vibration‐governed origin of isomer‐dependent RTP, enabling rational molecular design of long‐lived organic afterglow.








ABSTRACT
Structural isomerization has emerged as an effective strategy for improving the performance of organic room‐temperature phosphorescent materials, but reported explanations are mainly attributed to differences in molecular packing, spin‐orbit coupling, excited‐state electronic configurations, etc. The intrinsic vibrational differences encoded in the molecular structures of isomers, which may fundamentally govern triplet‐state excitons’ nonradiative behaviors, remain largely unexplored. Here, we construct five phosphorescent molecular structural isomerization pairs based on both purely hydrocarbon and heteroatom‐containing aromatic compounds, elucidating how regioisomerization redistributes local aromatic character and skeletal rigidity, thereby selectively suppressing the dominant dissipative vibrational modes (C═C and C─N) in the triplet state. This selective vibrational restriction effectively reduces nonradiative decay loss and ultimately determines the efficiency and lifetime of triplet excitons. The representative regioisomeric phosphor further demonstrates long‐lived bioimaging capability with an extended in vivo imaging window, highlighting the practical relevance of this design strategy. This work identifies dominant vibrational coordinates as the primary origin of isomer‐dependent RTP behaviors and establishes a vibrationally resolved mechanistic framework for excited‐state relaxation engineering.

title: One‐Step Access to Ultra‐Bright Macrocyclic Oligo‐BODIPYs Featuring Long‐Lived Cyclic Excitons
content:
Strong Fluorescence Meets Long Lifetimes: A template‐free, one‐step synthesis affords a series of methylene‐bridged macrocyclic oligo‐BODIPYs combining strong fluorescence with exceptionally long fluorescence lifetimes. Steady‐state and time‐resolved optical spectroscopy reveal unique excitonic coupling conditions and unusual size‐dependent photophysical trends. We rationalize our findings within a cyclic exciton model and hereby establish a versatile platform for the design of large functional fluorophore arrays.








ABSTRACT
The controlled organization of chromophores into defined assemblies with collective photophysical properties is a key concept for natural and artificial photonic systems. A template‐free, one‐step synthesis affords a series of methylene‐bridged macrocyclic oligo‐BODIPYs from readily available BODIPY precursors. Brønsted acid catalysis with paraformaldehyde as a C1 synthon links multiple BODIPY cores into β‐connected linear oligomers and macrocycles comprising up to twelve non‐conjugated chromophores. Optical spectroscopy and quantum chemical calculations provide initial insights into the photophysical mechanisms: steady‐state and time‐resolved spectroscopy reveal pronounced excitonic coupling across the chromophore arrays, which is confirmed by quantum chemical investigations at the simplified time‐dependent density functional theory level. The linear oligomers display typical J‐type characteristics, while the macrocyclic systems exhibit distinct multiband emission and unusual size‐dependent photophysical properties. Distinct excitonic regimes seem to coexist in the macrocyclic oligomers. Intense absorption bands are consistent with localized J‐coupled chromophore segments within the ring, while fluorescence can occur from J‐coupled segments and a lower‐lying cyclic exciton state with strongly reduced oscillator strength. In summary, our work establishes cyclic oligo‐BODIPYs as a versatile platform for investigating topology‐dependent excitonic phenomena, and also for developing functional superchromophores with tunable photophysical properties.

title: Radical Markovnikov Hydroboration of Unactivated Terminal Alkenes With HBaza‐Type Hydroborane via a Triple Catalysis
content:
A highly Markovnikov‐selective hydroboration of unactivated terminal alkenes with hydroboranes was developed, enabled by the synergistic interplay of photoredox, cobalt, and Brønsted acid catalysis. This methodology stands out for its broad substrate scope and good functional group tolerance.








ABSTRACT
Organoboron compounds are versatile building blocks for C─C and C–heteroatom bond formation, with broad applications in drug discovery and materials science. Hydroboration of alkenes with hydroboranes is a reliable route to access organoboron compoundsssssss, yet the Markovnikov‐selective hydroboration of unactivated terminal alkenes remains challenging. In this study, we report a triple catalysis strategy for the highly Markovnikov‐selective hydroboration of unactivated terminal alkenes with HBaza‐type hydroborane (HBaza: 1,3,2‐benzodiazaborolane). The reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope and good functional group compatibility, and has been successfully applied to the Markovnikov hydroboration of alkene derivatives from complex molecules. Further derivatizations of the resulting alkyl boron products, as well as the synthesis of biologically relevant molecules or intermediates, highlight the synthetic value of this method. Mechanistic studies support that this reaction proceeds via sequential metal‐hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)‐mediated radical generation and HBaza‐involved radical borylation process under a triple photoredox, cobalt, and Brønsted acid catalysis.

title: Tailoring Backbone Angles of Regioisomeric Covalent Organic Frameworks: Distinct O2 Adsorption Modes Enabling Efficient H2O2 Electrosynthesis
content:
Linkage‑angle engineering tailors backbone geometries of regioisomeric COFs to reconfigure oxygen‑surface interactions. The compact 60° framework of o‑TPDA‑COF favours Pauling‑type O2 adsorption, stabilizes OOH* intermediates, and enables high‑performance 2e− ORR toward efficient H2O2 electrosynthesis.








ABSTRACT
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) possess periodic skeletons and well‐defined catalytic sites, allowing precise molecular‐level regulation of interfacial properties in electrocatalytic oxygen reduction. However, conventional structural modifications fail to systematically tune oxygen adsorption geometry and interfacial electronic coupling. Here, we report a linkage‐angle engineering strategy that alters the bonding positions of reactive aldehyde groups to fabricate three regioisomeric COFs with predefined backbone dihedral angles of 180°, 120°, and 60°. The angle‑driven regioisomeric effect induces considerable differences in dipole moments together with uneven charge distribution. These collective structural features remodel oxygen‑surface interactions and modulate the intrinsic catalytic kinetics. Theoretical calculations confirm that the compact 60° framework of o‐TPDA‐COF reconstructs confined pore interfacial microenvironments. Unlike the Griffiths‑type oxygen adsorption favored in its angular analogues, molecular oxygen preferentially adopts the Pauling configuration within o‐TPDA‐COF to stabilize OOH* intermediates. Consequently, the optimal o‐TPDA‐COF reaches an excellent H2O2 productivity of 12.82 mol gcat−1 h−1 and a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 91.64%. This work realizes controllable modulation of oxygen‑adsorption behaviors in COF‑based 2e– oxygen reduction, delivering a novel geometry‑oriented design paradigm for porous electrocatalytic frameworks.

title: V─O─Ti Bridge‐Bond Polarity Boosts Na+ Migration in V‐Based Fluorophosphates for Fast Sodium Storage
content:
A bridge‐bond‐polarity‐driven strategy is proposed to enhance the electron exchange efficiency between V and O, while providing an exceptional environment for rapid Na+ transport. Thus, a synergistic enhancement of coupling between electronic structure and ion dynamics is achieved, yielding a fast‐charging capability at high C‐rates and a high energy density of 154 Wh kg−1 at the 9‐Ah scale.








ABSTRACT
Vanadium‐based fluorophosphates are promising high‐energy‐density cathodes for next‐generation sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs). However, the pronounced degradation of Na+ diffusion at high voltage hinders their fast‐charging capability. Herein, a Ti4+‐doping‐induced bridge‐bond‐polarity‐driven strategy is proposed to reshape the V electronic structure for facilitating V─O electron exchange. Correspondingly, voltage hysteresis, polarization, and structural distortion at high voltage are suppressed, accompanied by enhanced electronic conductivity. Meanwhile, the polar V─O─Ti bridge bonds expand the dominant one‐ and two‐dimensional Na+ transport channels by inducing bridging‐O displacement, further boosting Na+ migration capability. Therefore, Na3V1.92Ti0.08O(PO4)2F2 with V─O─Ti delivers high capacities of 121.8 and 62.1 mA h g−1 at 0.1C and 50C, respectively, while maintaining excellent cycling stability. Additionally, the 0.92‐Ah Na3V1.92Ti0.08O(PO4)2F2//HC pouch cell exhibits 80% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 1C. At the 9 Ah scale, the pouch cell achieves a high energy density of 154 Wh kg−1. This synergistic reinforcement strategy driven by bridge‐bond polarity paves the way for sustainable high‐power polyanionic SIBs.

title: Overcoming the Spin Barrier of Oxygen Redox Chemistry in Lithium–Oxygen Batteries via Metal–Support Magnetic Interaction
content:
The metal–support magnetic interaction endows Pd sites with intrinsic magnetic order, while an external magnetic field induces parallel spin alignment across adjacent Pd ensembles. This spin‐alignment system enables spin‐dependent electron transfer throughout the oxygen redox reaction, effectively suppressing 1O2 evolution and driving highly reversible Li–O2 batteries.








ABSTRACT
A major bottleneck for the practical application of lithium–oxygen (Li–O2) batteries is the high overpotential resulting from sluggish kinetics of oxygen redox chemistry. This kinetic limitation can rise in part from the spin‐state transition barriers in converting triplet oxygen (3O2) into peroxide species, alongside the parasitic generation of singlet oxygen (1O2). Here, we demonstrate that metal–support magnetic interactions can effectively overcome this spin barrier. Using palladium (Pd) nanoparticles anchored on ferrimagnetic CoFe2O4 (CFO) substrates as a model catalyst, we reveal that interfacial magnetic coupling restructures the spin and electronic states of Pd sites, generating spin‐polarized active ensembles with optimized adsorption toward oxygen intermediates. This interfacial spin‐electronic effect promotes the conversion of 3O2 into peroxide species while suppressing parasitic 1O2 evolution during charging, thereby improving the reversibility of oxygen redox chemistry. As a result, the Pd/CFO catalyst achieves a low charging overpotential of 0.05 V and remarkable energy efficiency (91.2%) under spin alignment. This finding establishes metal–support magnetic interaction as a powerful strategy for controlling spin‐dependent oxygen electrocatalysis, providing a general design principle for catalysts involving multi‐site interactions.

title: Unsaturated Carboxylates as Electrophilic Synthons for Transition‐Metal‐Catalyst‐Free Electroreductive Deoxygenative Coupling
content:
Saturated C─C bond formation from esters and alkyl halides conventionally requires two steps: Barbier‐Grignard ketone synthesis followed by Clemmensen or Wolff‐Kishner‐Huangminlon reduction. We report a one‐step electrochemical reductive coupling of aryl, alkenyl, and alkynyl carboxylates with alkyl halides to construct saturated C─C bonds. This mild, water‐ and air‐tolerant reaction features broad functional‐group compatibility and hundred‐gram scalability. Mechanistic studies support a radical‐radical cross‐coupling pathway.








ABSTRACT
The use of ester‐derived electrophiles in transition‐metal‐free electroreductive C(sp3)─C(sp3) bond formation remains largely unexplored. Herein, we report a sacrificial‐anode‐enabled electroreductive cross‐coupling of simple unsaturated carboxylates with unactivated alkyl halides. Aryl, alkenyl, and alkynyl carboxylates are readily incorporated, affording methylene‐bridged alkylarenes together with allylic and propargylic C(sp3)‐rich frameworks under mild conditions. Mechanistic studies support independent single‐electron reduction of both electrophilic partners, followed by radical‐radical coupling, alkoxide elimination, and cathodic deoxygenation via a Clemmensen‐like reduction pathway. This work establishes unsaturated carboxylates as a new class of alkylating reagents for electroreductive C(sp3)─C(sp3) bond formation.

title: Ultra‐Low Emission Cathode Recycling Enabled by Programmed Adaptive Pulse Joule Heating
content:
A programmed adaptive pulse Joule heating (PJH) strategy that exploits the intrinsic carbon in spent cathodes to regulate solid‐state reduction and drive selective lithium migration is reported. This process rapidly forms a Li2CO3‐rich surface, enabling over 96% lithium recovery by short‐duration water leaching without external reductants or acids, while demonstrating broad cathode compatibility and an ultra‐low greenhouse‐gas (GHG) footprint.








ABSTRACT
Sustainable recovery of valuable critical metals from spent lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs) is increasingly recognized as a cornerstone of global electrification and supply‐chain resilience. Joule‐heating technologies have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical routes; to advance this emerging electrothermal route, we integrate real‐time thermal feedback with reaction‐pathway regulation to reduce energy input, external reductant use, and greenhouse‐gas (GHG) emissions. Here, we develop a programmed adaptive pulse Joule heating (PJH) platform that transforms thermal reduction into a digitally guided and self‐regulating process. By maintaining an optimized temperature trajectory through adaptive current modulation, PJH promotes selective in situ reductive recovery via intrinsic carbon‐mediated pathways, with isotope‐tracing analysis supporting intrinsic carbon incorporation into carbonate products and life‐cycle assessment indicating a low GHG footprint of 2.90 kg CO2 eq. kg−1 under defined system boundaries. Under optimized conditions, battery‐grade lithium carbonate (> 99.5%), verified by product‐quality analysis, is selectively recovered via acid‐free rapid aqueous leaching (∼10 min) after seconds‐level (20 s) heat treatment without pretreatment. Preliminary scale‐up PJH demonstrations across diverse lithium‐containing resources suggest potential for broader application. These results demonstrate how adaptive PJH integrates thermal feedback with lower‐carbon process design, offering a potential route toward selective and low‐emission recycling of cathode materials.

title: Red Light‐Gated Charge Transfer Enables Trace Oxygen Response in Dye‐Sensitized TiO2–Carbon Nanotube Hybrids
content:
Light activation allows spatiotemporal control over materials, yet converting low‐energy red‐light excitation into chemically responsive electronic function remains challenging. Here we show that squaraine‐sensitized TiO2 domains embedded in single‐walled carbon nanotube networks generate a red‐light‐gated charge‐transfer state that reacts with O2. This enables chemiresistive trace O2 detection, with utility demonstrated in food‐spoilage monitoring.








ABSTRACT
Light offers a powerful means of activating materials with spatial and temporal precision. However, translating excited‐state processes into chemically responsive electronic function in conductive solids remains challenging, particularly under low‐energy red illumination. Herein, we report red light‐gated charge transfer in dye‐sensitized single‐walled carbon nanotube–TiO2 (SWCNT–TiO2) hybrids that enables trace oxygen detection. Immobilization of red‐absorbing squaraine sensitizers on TiO2 domains embedded within a conductive SWCNT network reversibly generates a photostationary charge‐transfer state under 628 nm excitation. Despite the low photon energy of red light, the hybrid architecture supports interfacial electron injection into TiO2 and hole accumulation in the nanotube scaffold, while remaining electronically dormant in the dark. Interception of photogenerated electrons by O2 perturbs this light‐induced state and converts excited‐state redox chemistry into a chemiresistive signal with ppb‐level sensitivity. This capability enables continuous monitoring of oxygen depletion in a sealed headspace during food spoilage. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, energy‐level alignment analysis, and charge‐carrier inversion experiments show that O2 triggers light‐activated changes in SWCNT carrier density. These findings demonstrate that low‐energy optical excitation can gate chemical response in dye‐sensitized SWCNT–TiO2 hybrids, establishing a design strategy for temporally controlled sensing and photoresponsive electronic function.

title: Suppressing Cathode Corrosion Induced by Impurity Cations in Alkaline Water Electrolyzers
content:
Impurity Fe species in electrolyte accelerate cathodic corrosion in alkaline electrolyzers by promoting peroxide formation. A strongly Lewis acidic CeOx protection layer stabilizes interfacial electronic structure via Fe−CeOx interactions, scavenges reactive oxygen species, and suppresses Fe accumulation, enabling stable Ni cathodes under universal industrial conditions.








ABSTRACT
In alkaline water electrolysis systems operated under industrial conditions, cations leaching from corrosive dissolution of the anode and balance‐of‐plant components progressively accumulate and contaminate the circulating electrolyte during prolonged operation. Here, we demonstrate for the first time that impurity cations, particularly Fe ions, compromise the long‐term structural stability of the Raney Ni cathode. The accumulation of Fe species on the cathode surface promotes the two‐electron reduction of crossover oxygen and the formation of HO2• radicals that drive oxidative corrosion of Ni sites. We then introduce a Lewis‐acidic CeOx layer on the cathode surface for protection. The layer effectively suppresses the reductive deposition of Fe on the cathode, while coordinatively unsaturated high‐valent Ce sites directly scavenge the reactive radicals. As a result, the protected Raney Ni cathode demonstrates marked stability in Fe‐containing electrolyte, maintaining stable operation over 3,500 h at 1.0 A cm−2 and 15,000 accelerated startup–shutdown cycles. Notably, this strategy exhibits strong feasibility and universality under practical operating conditions, maintaining stable cathode performance in the presence of up to 200 µM Fe(III) or various impurity cations derived from system components, including Co(II), Mn(II), Mo(VI), Cr(III), and Al(III).

title: Macrocyclization of ω‐Isocyano Aldehydes
content:
The ω‐isocyano aldehydes readily undergo cyclization to afford α‐acyloxy, α‐hydroxy, α‐acetamido, and α‐keto macrolactams, as well as tetrazole‐fused macrocycles, via C(sp3)─C(sp2) bond formation, providing access to diverse α‐functionalized medium‐sized lactams and macrolactams.








ABSTRACT
Medium‐sized rings and macrocycles constitute a privileged class of scaffolds in medicinal chemistry, providing unique access to challenging biological targets through their preorganized, semi‐rigid architectures. However, their synthesis remains challenging due to the unfavorable kinetic and thermodynamic constraints during ring closure. Herein, we report the efficient cyclization of ω‐isocyano aldehydes via Passerini and Ugi multicomponent reactions (MCRs), alongside related variants. These transformations provide rapid access to structurally diverse medium‐sized and macrocyclic α‐acyloxy, α‐hydroxy, α‐acetamido, and α‐keto lactams, as well as tetrazole‐fused macrocycles, under mild conditions. Notably, this macrocyclization strategy relies on C(sp3)─C(sp2) bond formation while simultaneously generating α‐functionalized amide motifs. By avoiding the need to pre‐synthesize α‐functionalized carboxylic acids, this approach offers a complementary alternative to traditional macrolactamization.

title: Hybridization‐Mediated Reversible sgRNA Caging Enables Tumor‐Selective Gene Editing for Potentiating Antitumor Immunity via cGAS Demethylation
content:
A tumor‐selective CRISPR/Cas9 system is developed by engineering a single‐stranded DNA containing apurinic/apyrimidinic sites (AP‐ssDNA) that blocks the target sgRNA upon hybridization. AP‐ssDNA/sgRNA is codelivered with Cas9 mRNA into tumors using biodegradable lipid nanoparticle. Overexpressed APE1 in tumor cells cleaves AP‐ssDNA to liberate the sgRNA, thus inducing tumor‐specific SUV39H1 gene editing to activate the cGAS‐STING pathway and enhance antitumor immunity.








ABSTRACT
Spatiotemporal precision remains a critical challenge against the gene editing technology used for disease treatment. We herein developed a tumor cell‐selective CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system by introducing a complementary single‐stranded DNA (ssDNA) containing apurinic/apyrimidinic (AP) sites (AP‐ssDNA) along the target region of single‐guided RNA (sgRNA). The engineered hybrid (AP‐ssDNA/sgRNA) could tracelessly release the native sgRNA in tumor cells due to cleavage of AP‐ssDNA by the overexpressed apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1), thus enabling tumor‐selective gene editing. Subsequently, a biodegradable lipid nanoparticle based on dynamic covalent bonding was developed to codeliver Cas9‐encoding mRNA (mCas9) with AP‐ssDNA/sgRNA targeting the SUV39H1 gene, which mediated silence of cyclic GMP‐AMP synthase (cGAS) methylation to activate stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and enhanced antitumor immunity. As thus, when coupled with radiotherapy, the gene editing platform provoked robust antitumor efficacy in B16F10 xenograft tumor‐bearing mice. This study provides a versatile paradigm for conditionally controlled gene editing and highlights the therapeutic potential of cGAS demethylation in reactivating cGAS‐STING pathway for antitumor immunotherapy.

title: Isolated Ir–Se Sites in Nickel Selenide for Glyoxal‐Mediated Ethylene Glycol Oxidation to Formate and PET Upcycling
content:
The electron‐withdrawing nature of the isolated Ir sites in NiSe modulates the electronic structure of neighboring Ni sites, promoting the formation of active NiOOH species. This electronic modulation facilitates bidentate adsorption of ethylene glycol, which is further oxidized to formate via the glyoxal‐mediated pathway.








ABSTRACT
The accumulation of plastic waste presents a persistent environmental challenge, motivating the development of strategies that integrate its remediation and upcycling. As a principal monomer derived from poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET), ethylene glycol (EG) serves as a key platform substrate for the electrochemical upcycling of PET waste into value‐added chemicals. In this study, nickel selenide (NiSe) was synthesized via pulsed laser irradiation in liquids, and atomically dispersed iridium (Ir) sites coordinated with selenium (Se) were introduced into the cationic sites of NiSe to regulate its intrinsic activity toward the electrocatalytic EG oxidation reaction. The Ir/NiSe‐2 catalyst oxidizes EG to formate via bidentate adsorption followed by a glyoxal‐mediated pathway, achieving a Faradaic efficiency of 83.09% at 1.60 V versus RHE, together with a formate yield rate of 1248 µmol cm−2 h−1. In situ Raman spectroscopy reveals an earlier onset of catalytically active NiOOH formation in Ir/NiSe‐2 compared to NiSe, evidencing Ir‐promoted modulation of the NiSe surface electronic structure. When coupled with Pt/C for the hydrogen evolution reaction in a two‐electrode configuration, the system sustains continuous electrolysis, producing formate and green hydrogen. After extended electrolysis, terephthalic acid and potassium diformate were recovered from the anolyte, demonstrating a viable route for PET upcycling into value‐added products.

title: Biomarker and Bioorthogonality Dual‐Locked Chemiluminescent Probes for Cancer Urine Test
content:
The tetrazine‐embedded chemiluminophores are devised to be non‐emissive even after phenolate formation, while a bioorthogonal reaction removes the tetrazine and abolishes the quenching pathway, restoring chemiluminescence. Accordingly, a dual‐locked chemiluminescent probe that requires both H2O2 activation and a bioorthogonal reaction is developed for sensitive tumor imaging and early urinary detection of lung metastases.








ABSTRACT
Bioorthogonality‐activatable optical imaging activates caged or quenched probes via bioorthogonal reactions for disease diagnosis. Although chemiluminescence enables low‐background detection, it has rarely been applied to bioorthogonality‐activatable imaging. Here, we synthesize chemiluminescent tetrazine probes (CLTZs) by coupling a tetrazine acceptor to a phenoxy‐1,2‐dioxetane donor through π‐conjugated vinylene linkers, enabling biomarker and bioorthogonality dual‐locked activation for cancer urine testing. Unlike conventional chemiluminophores, tetrazine in CLTZs mediates an internal‐conversion‐to‐a‐dark‐state quenching mechanism, suppressing chemiluminescence even after phenolate formation. Strong chemiluminescence is restored only when the phenolate form undergoes bioorthogonal reaction with bicyclononyne (BCN), generating pyridazine‐containing donor–π–acceptor chemiluminophores. This unique dark state enables development of an H2O2 and bioorthogonality dual‐locked probe (HBCP), emitting only when both H2O2 and BCN are present. By engineering BCN into a cancer‐activatable bioorthogonal urinary reporter (CBUR) that releases renal‐clearable BCN in tumors, a chemiluminescent bioorthogonal pair (HBCP & CBUR) is created. This pair achieves in vivo tumor imaging with a signal‐to‐background ratio of 438 and detects lung metastasis in early urinary assays with up to 23.9‐fold signal enhancement over healthy mice. This work provides a molecular design for bioorthogonality‐activatable chemiluminescence toward noninvasive, sensitive disease diagnosis.

title: Discovery of a Potent and Selective First‐In‐Class Antagonist of GPR15 With In Vivo Anti‐Obesity Activity
content:
Structural optimization led to the discovery of YL410, a potent, selective, and first‐in‐class antagonist targeting the atypical chemokine receptor GPR15. In diet‐induced obese (DIO) mice, treatment with YL410 elicited significant weight loss and robust glucose‐lowering effects.








ABSTRACT
GPR15 (G Protein‐coupled Receptor 15), an atypical chemokine receptor, is implicated in the pathogenesis of multiple diseases, yet small‐molecule GPR15 antagonists remain undeveloped. Herein, we identify and characterize YL410, the first‐in‐class potent and selective GPR15 antagonist. In the cAMP‐GloSensor assay, YL410 inhibits GPR15 with an IC50 of 0.027 ± 0.005 µM, and displays high selectivity against a panel of related GPCRs and kinases. It suppresses GPR15L‐induced Jurkat T‐cell migration, and exhibits favorable pharmacokinetics and acceptable safety. Molecular docking, replicated molecular dynamics simulations, quantitative contact analyses, and mutagenesis experiments support a plausible orthosteric binding model for YL410, maintained by a reproducible network of polar and hydrophobic contacts, which rationalizes its potent antagonism and observed structure–activity relationships (SAR). Complementary AI‐based structure predictions (AlphaFold3, Chai‐1, and Boltz) recapitulated the energetically accessible orthosteric poses but not the dynamically stable pose selected by the MD simulations, underscoring the importance of kinetic‐stability validation in antagonist pose selection. Notably, in a diet‐induced obesity (DIO) mouse model, YL410 administration induced significant weight loss and exerted blood glucose‐lowering effects. Collectively, this study presents the first potent, selective, and in vivo efficacious GPR15 antagonist, providing new insights into the development of therapeutics for the treatment of obesity.

title: Anion‐Dipole Catalytic Decomposition Enables Robust Solid Electrolyte Interfaces for Ah‐Level Aqueous Zinc Batteries
content:
Aromatic additives featuring high anion‐dipole binding energy (Eb) and electrostatic potential difference (ΔESP), exemplified by acetophenone (ACP), effectively achieve anion recognition and enrichment on the Zn anode interface, which reduces the anion decomposition energy barrier and constructs an inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interface (SEI), donating a high Zn plating/stripping coulombic efficiency and stable Ah‐level pouch cell cycling.








ABSTRACT
Constructing robust inorganic‐rich solid electrolyte interfaces (SEIs) without the compromised safety and interfacial kinetics remains challenging for aqueous zinc ion batteries. Herein, we identify anion‐dipole binding energy and electrostatic potential difference as double descriptors for screening trace additives as molecular captors for anions, and propose an anion‐dipole catalytic decomposition strategy to tailor the SEI. Specifically, electron‐deficient aromatic acetophenone preferentially enters the electrical double layer, selectively recognizing and concentrating anions. Concurrently, it catalyzes anion decomposition by accelerating bond‐cleavage kinetics and reducing activation free energy, forming the inorganic‐rich SEI. This tailored interface yields a high Zn2+ transference number (0.75), accelerates desolvation, and promotes planar (002)‐textured Zn deposition. Consequently, Zn//Zn symmetric cells exhibit exceptional cycling stability (7200 h), and an Ah‐level Zn//VO2 pouch cell with cathode mass loading of 20 mg·cm−2 delivers a capacity of 4.28 Ah at 0.2 A·g−1 and retains 88.9% of its initial capacity after 100 cycles at 1 A·g−1.

title: Modular Construction of Cyclic and Linear Quaternary Carbon Centers through Visible‐Light‐Induced Triplet Nitrene Transfer Reaction
content:
A visible light‐promoted formal semipinacol rearrangement of tertiary allyl alcohols using in situ‐generated triplet nitrene species as the initiator has been disclosed, enabling efficient construction of all‐carbon quaternary centers across various steric environments under redox‐neutral conditions, including rigid cyclic/spiro frameworks and flexible acyclic systems. Preliminary biological assessments of these β‐aminoketone derivatives revealed potent anti‐DENV‐2 activity.








ABSTRACT
All‐carbon quaternary centers represent a fundamental structural unit found in a wide range of functional molecules. Within the versatile synthetic toolbox, the semipinacol rearrangement (SPR) stands as one of the most powerful tools for assembling this sterically congested motif. In this context, ‌radical‐mediated SPR pathways‌, especially those entailing alkyl migrations, remain underexplored from a strategic standpoint. Herein, we report a visible light‐promoted formal SPR of tertiary allyl alcohols using in situ‐generated triplet nitrene species as the initiator under redox‐neutral conditions. This method demonstrates broad substrate scope, enabling efficient construction of all‐carbon quaternary centers across various steric environments, including rigid cyclic/spiro frameworks and flexible acyclic systems. Mechanistic investigations reveal substrate‐dependent pathways: alkenyl cyclobutanols undergo triplet nitrene addition followed by concurrent ring‐expansion and hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) to form cyclic ketones, while nonactivated allyl alcohols proceed through aziridination/ring‐opening/SPR sequences to produce linear β‐amino ketones. Preliminary biological assessments of these α‐quaternary β‐aminoketone derivatives revealed that compound 4a exhibited potent anti‐DENV‐2 activity, with an EC50 value of 0.95 ± 0.02 µM against viral replication.

title: Mitigating Surface Poisoning by Bidirectional Regulation for Efficient C1‐C2 Molecule Electrooxidation
content:
A Ga‐Ru dual‐promoter bidirectional regulation strategy was developed to optimize the electronic environment of the Pt active center to balance the dynamic adsorption of CO* and OH* to mitigate surface poisoning and thus achieve high performance for C1‐C2 molecule electrooxidation.








ABSTRACT
The rational design of Pt‐based electrocatalysts to alleviate CO intermediates poisoning during electrooxidation of C1‐C2 fuels (methanol, ethanol, formic acid) presents a grand challenge. Current detoxification strategies predominantly focus on enhancing OH* formation to accelerate CO* oxidation. However, the periodic voltage/current oscillations induced by accumulated OH species are often overlooked. Such accumulation of secondary poisoning intermediates inevitably leads to a high overpotential and poor operational stability. Herein, guided by machine learning screening, we resolve this dilemma by designing ultrathin PtPdGaRuFeMo high‐entropy alloy nanosheets featuring Ga and Ru dual‐promoter sites for the bidirectional regulation of CO* and OH* adsorption. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that the synergistic Ga and Ru sites modulate the electronic structure of active centers, balancing the dynamic adsorption of CO* and OH* to mitigate surface poisoning. Consequently, the as‐prepared catalysts deliver excellent specific activities of 5.4 mA cm−2 for methanol and 3.5 mA cm−2 for formic acid electrooxidation, surpassing commercial Pt/C by factors of 9.7 and 12.8, respectively. This study establishes a dual‐promoter bidirectional regulation, providing a promising route offering a robust solution to the stability‐activity trade‐off in fuel‐cell electrocatalysts.

title: S = 3/2 Iron(I)‐Bisphosphine‐Ate Complexes: Synthesis, Characterization, and Reactivity for Electrophile Activation
content:
In this work, we present a new class of unusual charged Fe(I)‐bisphosphine‐ates, along with full characterization of their structure and bonding, utilizing low‐temperature synthetic and spectroscopic and techniques. These complexes are highly reactive toward catalytically relevant electrophiles, and can serve as valuable synthons providing access to further transmetalated Fe(I)‐ate species.








ABSTRACT
Iron bisphosphine complexes represent an important class of sustainable catalysts for a variety of important chemical transformations due to the high abundance, low toxicity, and redox‐rich chemistry inherent to iron‐based systems. In particular, transient, low‐coordinate Fe(I) species are postulated to play a pivotal role in multiple catalytic transformations as the principal species for C─X bond activation (X = Cl, Br, I). However, insight into the electronic structure, bonding, and reactivity of Fe(I)‐bisphosphine complexes remains poorly developed. In the present study, we report the development of four‐coordinate (4C), high‐spin (S = 3/2) Fe(I)‐bisphosphine‐ates. Several novel Fe(I) complexes were structurally characterized, and their electronic structure and bonding were evaluated using a combined spectroscopic, synthetic, and computational approach. Additionally, this study highlights the potential role of charged species in synthetically relevant contexts via in situ formation of (4C) Fe(I)‐bisphosphine‐ates in the presence of ubiquitous additives (e.g. MgBr2). Lastly, we demonstrate the utility of these Fe(I)‐bisphosphine‐ates toward rapid C─X homolytic cleavage of common alkyl‐ and aryl‐halide electrophiles, as well as the ability to serve as synthons for further development of new high‐spin Fe(I)‐bisphosphine‐ate complexes through transmetalation.

title: Accessibility and Alignment of Trans‐Cleavage Substrates Modulate the Kinetics of Cas12a Ribonucleoprotein
content:
Two key binding events that collectively determine the catalytic efficiency of trans‐cleavage: (1) the substrate passing through the gap between the REC and NUC domains, determined by Kpass, and (2) the alignment of the substrate with the catalytic triad of the ribonucleoprotein, determined by Kalign. 








ABSTRACT
Mechanistic understanding of molecular interactions involved in the trans‐cleavage of CRISPR ribonucleoprotein systems is critical to advance genome editing, cell imaging, DNA nanotechnology, and molecular diagnostics. However, the mechanisms underlying molecular interactions of the substrate with the ribonucleoprotein are not clear. We report here molecular interactions that play critical roles in the trans‐cleavage activity of Cas12a ribonucleoproteins. We established kinetics models that quantitatively describe critical molecular interactions involving key functional domains of Cas12a ribonucleoproteins. Experimental validation of the enzyme kinetic models and quantitative determination of the apparent enzyme turnover number (k*cat) and Michaelis constant (K*M) enabled detailed studies of the accessibility and the alignment of the substrate with the catalytic site of the ribonucleoprotein. Consistent kinetic model predictions and experimental results indicate the critical importance of two processes: (1) the substrate passing through the gap between the REC (recognition) and NUC (nuclease) domains, determined by Kpass, and (2) the alignment of the substrate with the catalytic triad of the ribonucleoprotein, determined by Kalign. Guided by the kinetic models, rational design of substrates and activators enabled quantitative assessment of Kpass and Kalign. These results and fundamental understanding of the molecular interactions involved in the process provide a fundamental basis for improving the kinetics of CRISPR systems.

title: Mortise‐and‐Tenon Molecular Joint Covalent Organic Frameworks With Tunable Topology for Photothermal‐Catalytic Cross‐Dehydrogenative Coupling
content:
A “clip”‐like spacer induces ligand torsion and transforms a 2D framework into interpenetrated and noninterpenetrated 3D architectures, enabling tunable interpenetration, accessible active sites, and strong photothermal performance.








ABSTRACT
The controllable regulation of dimensionality and interpenetration in covalent organic frameworks (COFs) is crucial for optimizing photocatalytic performance, yet the translation of 3D COFs from structural construction to functional customization remains challenging. Here, we successfully designed a series of mortise‐and‐tenon molecular joint COFs by rationally engineering a twisted tetraphthaldehyde ligand bearing π‐conjugated “clips”. Stepwise extension of the “clips” enables topological evolution from 2D to twofold interpenetrated 3D, and ultimately to noninterpenetrated 3D structure. Notably, DHP‐CuPor‐COF with noninterpenetrated 3D structure amplifies light‐harvesting efficiency and substrate accessibility, enabling superior photothermal conversion and catalytic performance over its 2D and twofold interpenetrated 3D counterparts. To the best of our knowledge, it delivers highly efficient photothermal‐catalytic C─X (X = O, S) bond formation for selective transformation of phenolic compounds via cross‐dehydrogenative coupling (CDC) reactions (conv., >90% and yield, >80%), markedly outperforming conventional thermal catalysis. The high efficiency arises from the synergistic of open 3D channels, abundant Cu‐porphyrin active sites and strong photothermal effect. This work provides an innovative strategy to tune the topological chemistry of COFs for advanced photocatalytic applications.

title: Hydrophobic Microphase Separation‐Driven Polycondensation and Carbonization for the Formation of Carbonized Polymer Dots
content:
The hydrothermal synthesis of carbonized polymer dots (CPDs) proceeds via a polymerization–carbonization pathway that is driven by hydrophobic microphase separation. Originating from the unique core‐shell architecture of CPDs, this hydrophobic microphase reduces local water availability, thereby shifting reversible dehydration‐mediated equilibria forward and promoting further polymerization and carbonization. This mechanistic understanding inspires a new strategy for tuning CPDs size.








ABSTRACT
Hydrothermal synthesis has been widely used to prepare carbonized polymer dots (CPDs) in a one‐pot manner, yet how initial precursors evolve into nanoparticles in water‐rich environments remains poorly understood. Here, hydrophobic microphase separation is identified as a microenvironmental mechanism governing CPDs formation. CPDs are proved to possess a hydrophobic core and a hydrophilic shell, consistent with nanoscopic domains of reduced water accessibility during hydrothermal growth. These hydrophobic microphases locally shift reversible dehydration equilibria toward water loss, particularly dehydrative condensation, thereby sustaining polycondensation, crosslinking, and carbonization. The resulting microphase‐promoted dehydration process drives the nucleation and growth of CPDs. By independently tuning monomer hydrophobicity and crosslinking confinement, mechanism‐guided regulation of CPDs size and product fraction is achieved. These findings establish microphase‐promoted dehydration as a chemical principle for the rational hydrothermal synthesis of carbon nanomaterials.

title: dsRADAR: Imaging and Detecting Cellular dsRNA by Repurposing RNA‐Binding Proteins
content:
Double‐stranded RNA (dsRNA) plays an important role in the innate immune system, but can be misregulated in disease, leading to inflammation. Despite the importance of this motif, methods for detecting dsRNA remain limited. This work shows that ADAR3 can be repurposed to provide improved detection of dsRNA, which is demonstrated in the context of viral infection and inflammation. 








ABSTRACT
Double‐stranded RNA (dsRNA) is recognized by cellular receptors as a sign of viral infection, triggering the innate immune response. Cellular dysregulation can also lead to accumulation of endogenously produced dsRNA that stimulates a viral‐like immune response. Additionally, dsRNA contamination in RNA therapeutics can lead to harmful side effects via a similar pathway. Despite the clinical relevance of dsRNA, reliable tools for its detection remain limited. Currently, dsRNA detection relies almost exclusively on the monoclonal antibodies J2 and K1, which suffer from sequence bias and low sensitivity. To address this challenge, we repurposed naturally occurring dsRNA‐binding domains (dsRBDs) to produce reliable, pan‐specific affinity reagents for dsRNA. We systematically screened the dsRBDs of the three human adenosine deaminases acting on RNA (ADARs) and identified ADAR3 dsRBDs as the most promising candidates. We then engineered ADAR3‐derived dsRBD constructs having varying linker lengths and domain combinations to create dsRNA accumulation detected by ADAR3 RBDs (dsRADAR) affinity reagents. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of dsRADAR over currently available dsRNA antibodies in a cell model of viral infection and a tissue model of gastric inflammation. Together, dsRADAR provides a sensitive and reliable approach for imaging and detecting diverse dsRNA structures in biological contexts.

title: Ultrathin b‐Oriented Co‐Gallate MOF Membranes for Lithium Recovery: Precise Ion Sieving via Geometry‐Confined Dehydration
content:
An ultrathin, b‐oriented Co‐gallate (ub‐CoG) metal–organic framework membrane, fabricated via a gas–liquid interfacial soft‐template strategy, features zigzag subnanochannels that geometrically confine ion dehydration, enabling K+ to outpace Li+, Na+, and Mg2+ during permeation and delivering a record K+/Li+ selectivity of 13.5 for lithium recovery from salt‐lake brines.








ABSTRACT
Selective K+ over Li+ separation is indispensable for lithium recovery from salt‐lake brines, whereas simultaneous high‐efficiency separation of K+ from interfering Na+ and Mg2+ cations remains challenging for pristine MOF membranes. Herein, an ultrathin b‐oriented Co‐gallate MOF membrane is fabricated using a gas–liquid interfacial soft‐template approach. The membrane possesses 3D interconnected zigzag subnanochannels (≈3.7 Å) that impose geometry‐confined ion dehydration, hindering the transport of Li+, Na+, and Mg2+ far more significantly than K+, as corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations. Under a concentration gradient driving force, the ub‐CoG membrane achieves a prominent K+/Li+ selectivity of 13.5, as well as excellent K+/Na+ and K+/Mg2+ sieving capability. The recorded K+/Li+ selectivity stands as the highest value among MOF ion‐sieving membranes. This interfacial orientation strategy provides a promising pathway to advanced ion‐sieving membranes for multicomponent industrial brine lithium extraction.

title: RNA Organelles in DNA‐Based Artificial Cells Provide Spatial Aptamer Functions and Enhanced Signal Processing
content:
Multiphase DNA–RNA artificial cells integrate a protective DNA shell, a transcriptionally active DNA core, and a functional RNA organelle. Spatial compartmentalization enables signal generation, external protein expression, and selective recapture via RNA aptamers. 








ABSTRACT
Naturally occurring biomolecular condensates orchestrate key cellular processes by creating spatially distinct reaction environments, yet engineering synthetic condensates that combine structural programmability with spatioselectively encoded function remains challenging. Here, we report multiphase DNA–RNA artificial cells (ACs) that embed functional RNA condensates as organelle‐like compartments within programmable DNA core–shell ACs. A single thermal assembly protocol yields three‐phase ACs comprising a glassy RNA core organelle embedded in a liquid‐like DNA compartment, surrounded by a crosslinked DNA shell. The RNA organelles contain aptamer function, enabling selective protein recruitment and small‐molecule activation, while the DNA scaffold provides independent addressability, modulates RNA‐condensate size, and enhances resistance to serum‐mediated degradation. We further show that RNA chemistry can be used to adjust environmental responsiveness: unmodified RNA organelles undergo rapid degradation in serum and release captured protein cargo, whereas 2′‐fluoro‐modified RNA organelles remain stable for at least 24 h. Finally, by coupling transcriptional modules localized in the DNA core to cell‐free protein translation in the surrounding medium, we establish sender–receiver communication between AC populations and self‐actuating signal processing within individual DNA–RNA ACs. These results establish hybrid nucleic‐acid ACs as programmable, spatially organized systems that couple compartment architecture, RNA molecular recognition, and biochemical communication.

title: Aromaticity Engineering of Hybrid Cyanine Dyes for Metabolic Labeling and Bioorthogonal NIR‐II Imaging of Gut Microbiota
content:
In this study, we removed heteroatoms from the classical Si‐xanthene structure and effectively integrated the more planar and conjugated aminofluorene with the cyanine dye skeleton, enhancing the molecular aromaticity in the excited state, successfully constructing novel hybrid cyanine dyes IF with NIR‐II emission, excellent photostability, and high brightness. By adjusting the steric hindrance and ICT effect, the quantum yield of IFPy is 49 times higher than that of IFQ. Based on this, we developed a new NIR‐II bioorthogonal probe to achieve specific imaging of intestinal bacteria and explored the influence of host environment of diabetes on the spatial distribution of intestinal bacteria.








ABSTRACT
In the context of diabetes, host immune dysfunction and microcirculation damage significantly increase the susceptibility to bacterial infection. Therefore, the development of high‐performance molecular imaging tools to dynamically track the migration and colonization of bacteria in deep living tissues is crucial to distinguish pathology‐associated behavioral changes. In this study, we removed heteroatoms from the classical xanthene structure and effectively integrated the more planar and conjugated aminofluorene with the cyanine dye skeleton, enhancing the molecular aromaticity in the excited state, successfully constructing novel hybrid cyanine dyes IF with NIR‐II emission, excellent photostability, and high brightness. Among them, the quantum yield of IFPy is 49 times higher than that of IFQ. Based on this, we developed a new NIR‐II bioorthogonal probe to achieve specific imaging of intestinal bacteria and explored the influence of host environment of diabetes on the spatial distribution of intestinal bacteria. This work provides new insights into the design of fluorescent dyes and imaging of gut microbiota.

title: Interfacial Electron–Proton Dual Modulation of Fe Single‐Atom Catalyst by α‐MoC for O2 Activation and Lignin Depolymerization
content:
Interfacing α‐MoC nanoparticles with Fe–N4 single‐atom sites couples electron and proton regulation, increasing the apparent O2‐activation Vmax 2.8‐fold. Electron withdrawal weakens *OH adsorption, while accelerated water dissociation supplies local protons for *OH‐to‐H2O conversion. The resulting nearly four‐electron pathway suppresses reactive oxygen species (ROS) and drives native birch lignin depolymerization under mild alkaline conditions, offering a versatile strategy for biomass valorization.








ABSTRACT
Efficient O2 activation under mild conditions is central to oxidative biomass valorization, yet single‐atom catalysts often suffer from sluggish proton‐coupled oxygen intermediate conversion, particularly because of overly strong *OH adsorption. Inspired by the cooperative electron and proton management in cytochrome c oxidase, we report an α‐MoC/Fe–N4 catalyst in which α‐MoC nanoparticles are interfaced with Fe–N4 single‐atom sites on a nitrogen‐doped carbon scaffold. The α‐MoC component plays a dual role: it withdraws electron density from Fe sites to weaken oxygen‐intermediate adsorption and promotes water dissociation to provide local protons for *OH‐to‐H2O conversion. As a result, α‐MoC/Fe–N4 exhibits a 2.8‐fold higher Vmax for O2 activation than Fe–N4 and proceeds through a nearly four‐electron oxygen reduction pathway with negligible reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. This interfacial strategy is generalizable to various M–N–C single‐atom catalysts, including Mn, Co, Ni, Cu, Sn, Ir, and Pt. Enabled by efficient O2 activation, α‐MoC/Fe–N4 depolymerizes native birch lignin under mild alkaline conditions, substantially decreasing its molecular weight and cleaving β–O–4, β–β, and β–5 linkages. This work establishes an electron‐proton dual‐modulation strategy for constructing high‐performance single‐atom catalysts for biomass conversion.

title: Water‐Mediated Reversible Crystalline Phase Transformation Enables Color Switching and Circularly Polarized Luminescence Handedness Inversion
content:
A hydration/dehydration‐driven crystal‐to‐crystal transformation reconfigures molecular packing and supramolecular chirality in ionic crystals, enabling reversible emission‐color modulation and CPL handedness inversion.








ABSTRACT
Stimuli‐responsive circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) modulation is highly sought for adaptive chiroptical systems, yet achieving reversible CPL handedness inversion in crystalline solids remains challenging. Here, we report organic ionic crystals composed of luminescent cations and chiral anions that undergo crystal‐to‐crystal transformations through hydration/dehydration cycling. These transformations induce in situ switching between yellow and red emission, accompanied by complete inversion of CPL handedness. Structural analyses reveal that reversible changes in lattice hydration reorganize the supramolecular architecture from a double‐helical hydrogen‐bonded framework to a single‐helical architecture with opposite helicity, while simultaneously reshaping chromophore packing. Theoretical investigations further show that this structural reconfiguration alters intermolecular electronic delocalization and reorients the electric and magnetic transition dipole moments, with the angle between them crossing the critical 90° threshold, thereby accounting for the inversion of both circular dichroism and CPL responses. The reversible optical response is robust over multiple switching cycles, and can be spatially patterned to generate multidomain CPL heterostructures, highlighting its potential for multi‐parameter photonic encoding. This work offers fundamental insight into hydration‐regulated chiral transfer in molecular crystals, and establishes a design platform for adaptive chiroptical materials.

title: Generation of Tailorable Multi‐Property Molecules via Multimodal Spectral Fusion Evolution
content:
The MUltimodal Spectral fusion Evolution (MUSE) framework treats infrared, Raman, x‐ray absorption, ultraviolet–visible, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectra as a unified chemical language. Spectral fusion and spectra‐to‐molecule decoding enable controllable molecular generation across structural, physicochemical, and electronic objectives, achieving up to 700‐fold enrichment of rare multi‐property candidates.








ABSTRACT
Molecular generation stands at the forefront of intelligent molecular design, promising transformative advances in the discovery of molecules that meet drug‐likeness or catalysis requirements. However, existing generative models typically focus on optimizing a single target property at a time, hindered by the intrinsic difficulty of simultaneously encoding and evolving multiple structural features. Herein, we developed MUltimodal Spectral fusion Evolution (MUSE)—a spectroscopy‐guided generative framework that unifies multimodal spectroscopic descriptors as a universal chemical language for multi‐property molecular creation. A Spectra‐to‐Molecule (S2M) model, as one of MUSE's core modules, achieved a high success rate in molecular structure generation by training on a self‐built density functional theory (DFT) level multimodal spectral database. Leveraging the continuously variable nature of spectral descriptors, MUSE achieved synergistic integration of structural, vibrational, and electronic information by combining complementary spectroscopic modalities. Through evolutionary algorithms that constrain the generation direction of multi‐property molecules, the framework enables up to 700‐fold enrichment of rare quadruple‐property candidates. This work provides a scalable pathway for multi‐objective discovery in chemistry and materials science.

title: A DNA G‐Quadruplex‐Targeting Ligand Suppresses c‐MYC Expression: Implications for Gemcitabine‑Resistant Pancreatic Cancer
content:
PQB‐4, a fluorescent small‐molecule ligand that targets c‐MYC DNA G‐quadruplexes (G4s), showed marked synergy with gemcitabine in resistant PANC‐1 cells (CI = 0.027). In vivo, the ligand reduced tumor weight by 44% in a PANC‐1 xenograft model. These results highlight the therapeutic potential of c‐MYC DNA G4‐targeting ligands for treating gemcitabine‐resistant pancreatic cancer. 








ABSTRACT
The MYC oncogene is dysregulated in nearly 70% of human cancers and plays a central role in tumor initiation and progression. However, direct targeting of c‐MYC remains challenging because of its “undruggable” nature. Stabilization of DNA G‐quadruplex (G4) structures within the c‐MYC promoter offers an alternative strategy to suppress c‐MYC transcription. Here, we report the synthesis and biological evaluation of a series of styryl quinolinium ligands, identifying PQB‐4 as a selective c‐MYC DNA G4‐binder (KD <1.0 µM). PQB‐4 exhibited marked antiproliferative activity against pancreatic cancer cell lines, including MIA PaCa‐2 (IC50 = 2.9 µM), PANC‐1 (IC50 = 4.5 µM), and gemcitabine‐resistant PANC‐1 cells (IC50 = 5.0 µM), while showing substantially lower toxicity toward noncancerous HK‐2 cells (IC50 = 40.1 µM). Mechanistically, PQB‐4 stabilized c‐MYC DNA G4‐structures, suppressed c‐MYC mRNA and protein expression, induced G0/G1 cell‐cycle arrest, and activated a p53‐dependent DNA damage response. PQB‐4 also promoted telomere damage, cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, ferroptosis, and mitophagy, while inhibiting cancer cell migration, proliferation, and survival. Notably, PQB‐4 synergized strongly with gemcitabine in resistant PANC‐1 cells (CI = 0.027). In a PANC‐1 xenograft model, PQB‐4 reduced tumor weight by 44%. These findings highlight c‐MYC DNA G4 targeting by PQB‐4 as a feasible therapeutic strategy for pancreatic cancer, particularly in gemcitabine‐resistant disease.

title: Click‐to‐Release Reactivity of Quaternary Anilinium Tetrazines Enables Cascade Assembly of Multifunctional Biomolecular Scaffolds
content:
Click chemistry has evolved from making covalent connections to also breaking bonds. Here, a cascade assembly is reported that combines these maneuvers to build multifunctional biomolecular scaffolds in a modular one‐pot reaction. The unifying azide release‐tetrazine hub clicks with a trans‐cyclooctene tag, rapidly liberates N,N‐dimethylaniline to generate a thiol trap in situ, and finishes by adding a strained alkyne building block, all in high yield.








ABSTRACT
Click chemistry has evolved from its origins in forming covalent connections to also include breaking bonds, cleaving linkers, and liberating cargo, creating broad applications in chemical biology and biomedicine. The reaction sequences that drive these tools are complex, and thus prone to an array of dead‐end intermediates that reduce their release/cleavage efficiency. Here, we redirect that complexity to explore yet another aspect of tetrazine (Tz)/trans‐cyclooctene (TCO) click‐to‐release. By exchanging the carbamate linkage of established release Tzs for an anilinium leaving group, post‐click tautomerization is accelerated and temporally synchronized, generating an intermediate capable of trapping thiols rapidly and in high yields. Further integration of an orthogonal azide into the Tz hub enables a one‐pot multi‐component reaction that allows straightforward combinatorial synthesis of densely functionalized architectures. Leveraging both click and release, the resulting process converts a Tz/TCO pair into a ternary scaffold on demand, readily incorporating fluorophores, chelators, cleavable drugs, proteins, oligonucleotides, and more. This modular cascade assembly offers a rapid and versatile platform for functionalization of biomolecules and small molecule targeting vectors, with immediate potential in imaging, theranostics, and multivalent bioconjugate design.

title: Breaking the Additive Paradox in Aqueous Aluminum‐Ion Batteries via Weak‐Coordination Asymmetric Electrolyte Chemistry
content:
Beyond the trade‐off: electrolyte optimization can redistribute rather than eliminate failure. In the weak‐coordination asymmetric electrolyte (Al(OTf)3–DMSO–FEC), DMSO reconstructs the rigid Al3+ hydration environment but leaves a secondary dielectric/interfacial bottleneck, which is subsequently compensated by FEC through enhanced electrostatic screening and fluorinated interphase formation. This sequential resolution of coupled failure modes enables 2000 h reversible Al plating/stripping and 90.8% capacity retention after 2000 cycles.








ABSTRACT
Aqueous aluminum‐ion batteries (AAIBs) are compelling for sustainable storage, yet the strong hydrolysis of Al3+ acidifies the electrolyte, causing corrosion and passivation that necessitate modification. Additives designed to break the rigid Al3+ solvation shell face a paradox: they often compromise reversibility via either dielectric collapse or kinetic deadlocks. Here, we break this paradox by establishing a weak‐coordination asymmetric electrolyte based on aluminum trifluoromethanesulfonate (Al(OTF)3), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC). DMSO coordinates to Al3+, displacing coordinated water to suppress water activity, but cannot preserve the dielectric environment. FEC compensates via three synergistic functions: high dielectric constant for electrostatic screening, weak hydrogen bonding for solvation asymmetry reinforcement, and reductive decomposition for solid electrolyte interphase(SEI) formation. The sequential coupling of DMSO‐mediated solvation disruption with FEC‐enables dielectric/interfacial compensation accelerates desolvation and stabilizes electrode: a fluorinated SEI enables 2000 h reversible Al plating/stripping, while a spinel‐to‐layer transformation creates a fluorinated interface on vanadium oxide with asymmetric channels, mitigating dissolution. The full cell retains 90.8% capacity after 2000 cycles at 4 A g−1. By showing that resolving one bottleneck can expose another, this work reframes additive optimization as sequential processes of identifying and compensating coupled failure mechanisms, generalizing a design principle for multivalent aqueous electrolytes.

title: The tRNA‐Modification Geranyl‐2‐Thiouridine Enables RNA‐Lipid Association
content:
We report the preparation of mono‐ to tri‐geranylated RNA and the association of the hydrophobic RNA with membranes for future efficient incorporation of RNA into liposomes.








ABSTRACT
The packaging of RNA in lipid nanoparticles for protection and delivery was key for the development of mRNA vaccines and therapeutics. Formulation requires the addition of a variety of lipids (including cationic) in high amounts to form complexes with the negatively charged RNA. While this approach was successful for the development of RNA vaccines, it represents a major challenge for future developments. Increasing the lipophilicity of RNA is one possible approach to reducing the amount of lipid required. In nature, geranyl‐2‐thiouridine occurs at the “Wobble” position 34 of certain bacterial tRNAs. This work details investigations into geranylated oligonucleotides and their interactions with lipids. We developed an efficient post‐synthetic procedure for oligonucleotide geranylation in aqueous solutions using a geranyl‐sulfonium salt. We discovered that the geranyl‐modification can be replaced by thiol‐nucleophiles, enabling a reversible switch of the hydrophobic character of the oligonucleotides. We show that the geranyl‐modified oligonucleotides anchor onto neutral membrane structures and oil droplets. Oligonucleotides bound to the outer surface of neutral liposomes can flip to the inner membrane surface by freeze‐thaw cycles, leading to a protective effect against enzymatic or chemical degradation. Our work expands the scope of oligonucleotide lipidation strategies, which are of great interest in RNA delivery systems.

title: Supramolecular Polymerization of Triphenylamine[3]arenes for Switchable and Stimuli‐Responsive Chiroptical Properties
content:
Embedding triphenylamine[3]arenes with chiral peripheries directs their self‐assembly into chiral supramolecular polymers with intense blue circularly polarized luminescence. This system integrates reversible acid–base switching and irreversible photo‐triggered radical generation, revealing a “confinement effect” that enables spatiotemporal control over supramolecular chirality.








ABSTRACT
The design of advanced photonic materials with integrated stimuli‐responsive properties remains coveted yet challenging. Herein, we demonstrate that chiral supramolecular assembly of triphenylamine[3]arenes (TPA[3]s) offers an efficient and modular solution to address this challenge. Despite intrinsically nonplanar and conformationally flexible macrocyclic scaffold, peripheral chiral alkyl chains direct TPA[3]s to self‐assemble into long‐range one‐dimensional (1D) nanofibers, as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy, ultimately giving rise to intense blue circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) with a glum of 1.2 × 10−3 and a fluorescence quantum yield of 48%. Benefiting from the triphenylamine cores, the resulting supramolecular polymers exhibit reversible CPL switching upon acid–base stimulation. Notably, TPA[3]s readily undergo rapid photo‐induced radical generation in dilute monomeric solution, whereas this process is significantly suppressed in the supramolecular assemblies due to molecular confinement. Combining spectroscopic analyses with coarse‐grained molecular dynamics simulations reveals that the formation of air‐stable TPA radical cations disrupts the chiral packing, leading to disassembly of supramolecular polymers and the concomitant irreversible loss of CD and CPL signals. These findings establish supramolecular polymerization as a versatile strategy for organizing macrocyclic arenes into ordered 1D chiral assemblies with multi‐responsive CPL properties, while providing general design principles for photoresponsive chiral optoelectronic systems.

title: Raman Self‐Tracking Copper Metal‐Organic Framework‐Based Nanoplatform for Cuproptosis Cancer Therapy
content:
An antitumor nanoplatform based on copper metal‐organic framework. The nanoplatform responsively degrade under H2O2 in the tumor microenvironment, releasing Cu2+ to induce tumor cuproptosis and aromatic aldehydes to synergistically eradicate tumors. Moreover, the nanoplatform possesses self‐tracking capability, and its distribution and release can be visualized by Raman imaging.








ABSTRACT
Cuproptosis represents a promising strategy for cancer therapy, yet its clinical translation is hampered by unexpected deactivation and off‐target toxicity of copper ions during their delivery to tumors. We developed a copper metal‐organic framework‐based nanoplatform (CuF) with H2O2 responsiveness and Raman self‐tracking capability for cuproptosis‐mediated antitumor therapy. CuF was prepared by coordinating Cu2+ with an alkyne‐bearing ligand, followed by PEGylation and incorporation of an iron‐based catalyst. CuF undergoes catalyst‐mediated oxidative cleavage of alkynyl bonds under tumor‐associated elevated H2O2 levels, causing CuF degradation and Cu2+ release. Released Cu2+ causes copper overload in tumor cells, thereby inducing potent cuproptosis. Meanwhile, the resultant aldehydes and acids generated by the oxidative cleavage of alkynes can further synergistically potentiate cuproptosis. Consequently, CuF demonstrated high antitumor efficacy in a 4T1 tumor‐bearing mouse model (with a tumor inhibition rate of 91%). Moreover, alkynes in the metal‐organic framework (MOF) backbone provided an intrinsically enhanced Raman signal, enabling label‐free self‐tracking of CuF distribution and degradation in cells and tissue sections through Raman imaging. Overall, this work not only provides a new paradigm for cuproptosis‐based anticancer agents, but also offers a versatile strategy for engineering H2O2 responsive materials and Raman imaging nanoplatforms.

title: Molecular Gating of the Reactive Water Topological Network for Stable Aqueous Zn Batteries
content:
A molecular gating strategy that targets hydrogen‐bond connectivity has been proposed for regulating the reactive water field in aqueous electrolytes. The HBN‐gated electrolyte fragments the percolated water network into low‐cooperativity domains, suppressing proton‐relay HER and stabilizing the Zn electrodeposition field, enabling highly reversible Zn anodes and durable 1.0 Ah‐level NVO||Zn pouch cells. This hydrogen‐bond gating concept establishes a transferable design principle for controlling reactive aqueous environments in metal batteries and other electrochemical systems.








ABSTRACT
The instability of aqueous Zn batteries originates not only from the intrinsic reactivity of water, but also from the continuous hydrogen‐bonded network that enables cooperative interfacial degradation. In conventional aqueous electrolytes, this percolated water network supports proton relay, hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), local alkalization, by‐product precipitation, and Zn2+ flux distortion, thereby forming a self‐amplifying failure loop at the Zn/electrolyte interface. Herein, we propose a molecular gating strategy to regulate this reactive water network using 4‐hydroxy‐2‐butanone (HBN) as a dual‐site hydrogen‐bond modulator. The carbonyl and hydroxyl groups of HBN competitively interact with water, fragmenting the continuous H2O–H2O hydrogen‐bond network into low‐cooperativity water domains and suppressing proton‐relay HER. Concurrently, HBN mildly reshapes the Zn2+ solvation sheath environment toward a less water‐dominated configuration, moderating interfacial charge‑transfer while preserving essential Zn2+ transport. This topology‐gated aqueous regime simultaneously suppresses water‐induced side reactions, prevents alkaline passivation‐driven Zn2+ flux distortion, and enables compact Zn deposition. Consequently, the optimized electrolyte affords highly reversible Zn plating/stripping with an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.12% over 800 cycles and supports a 1.0 Ah‐level NVO||Zn pouch cell for 70 cycles with negligible capacity decay.

title: A Two‐Dimensional Organic Salt With a Deep‐Ultraviolet Cutoff Edge and Strong Second‐Harmonic Generation
content:
The organic guanidinium salt [C(NH2)3][CH3(CH2)3BF3] exhibits rare coexistence of a deep‐UV cutoff edge, strong second harmonic generation response, moderate birefringence, and calculated phase‐matching wavelength covers its optical transparency range.








ABSTRACT
Targeted synthesis of ultraviolet (UV) nonlinear optical (NLO) materials, especially organic salts, has experienced considerable difficulties due to the stringent requirement that these materials simultaneously possess ultra‐wide UV transparency, strong second‐harmonic generation (SHG), and short SHG phase‐matching cutoff wavelength. We report herein the designed synthesis of the first deep‐UV‐transparent NLO organic guanidinium salt [C(NH2)3][CH3(CH2)3BF3], featuring a honeycomb‐layered structure with uniformly aligned π‐conjugated [C(NH2)3]+ cations. The compound possesses a deep‐UV cutoff edge (197 nm), strong SHG responses at both 1064 nm (4.5 × KH2PO4) and 532 nm (0.7 × β‐BaB2O4), and sufficient birefringence (0.12 @ 546 nm). The calculated phase‐matching wavelength fully covers its optical transparency range (extending down to 197 nm), confirming that [C(NH2)3][CH3(CH2)3BF3] is a very promising UV NLO material. Theoretical calculations and crystal structure analysis show that the rare coexistence of optimal performance in the key optical properties can be attributed to an ideal two‐dimensional layered structure, combined with the π‐conjugated [C(NH2)3]+ cations and the flexible [CH3(CH2)3BF3]− anions. This research affords a new paradigm for the designed synthesis of high‐performance UV NLO organic salts.

title: Cross‐Dimensional Coupled Atomic Insights Into Structural Degradation of Pt‐Alloy Oxygen Reduction Reaction Catalysts
content:
Elucidation for the degradation mechanism of Pt‐alloy ORR catalyst through a cross‐dimensional coupling of AET, in situ x‐ray and theoretical calculations.








ABSTRACT
Achieving an atomic‐scale comprehensive understanding is crucial for the decipherment of nanocatalyst degradation pathways​ and guidance in rational design of durable catalysts. In this work, cross‐dimensional coupled atomic‐scale structural degradation mechanism of representative compound PtZn nanoalloy during oxygen reduction reaction electrocatalysis was comprehensively interrogated by integrating the atomic electron tomography (AET), synchrotron x‐ray techniques, and theoretical calculations. In situ x‐ray measurements demonstrated a globally stable face‐centered tetragonal bulk structure during continuous cycling; at the real three‐dimensional atomic level, further AET observations revealed significant localized surface degradation characterized by inhomogeneous Pt segregation, lattice transition, bond length expansion, coordination number reduction, and increased normal strain. These synergistic experimental results demonstrate a phenomenon of inhomogeneous structure degradation, revealing how dynamic interfacial change and bulk lattice stability propagate localized compositional heterogeneity: significant guidance to synthesize defect‐tolerant Pt skin against Zn dissolution. Corroborated by theoretical calculations, our findings established that the Pt segregation and structural transformation on the surface and sub‐surface of the catalyst were the energy‐driven degradation pathways and played important roles in the sustained deactivation of the catalyst. By integration of cross‐dimensional information, we link surface atomic heterogeneity on the surface of individual particles, overall structural changes of the catalyst and catalytic performance.

title: Synthesis of Enones and Enals From Alkenes via Alkenyl Thianthrenium Salts
content:
Herein, we report a two‐step procedure for the stereoselective conversion of mono‐, di‐ and trisubstituted alkenes into enones and enals via a combined alkenyl C–H bond functionalization and carbonylative cross‐coupling approach using alkenyl thianthrenium salts (alkenyl–TT salts).








ABSTRACT
Herein, we show the stereoselective conversion of alkenes into enones and enals. Alkenyl thianthrenium salts are used as a readily accessible pool of stereodefined alkenyl electrophiles that can be engaged in two types of carbonylative Pd‐catalyzed three‐component coupling reactions. Using alkyl zinc species generated in situ from alkyl iodides, enones can be accessed via a carbonylative Negishi coupling. In the presence of triethylsilane, enals can be generated via reductive carbonylation.

title: Coking–Crosslinking Competition Shapes Alveolar Hard Carbon Formation From Heterogeneous Precursors for Wide‐Temperature Sodium Storage
content:
Coking‐crosslinking competition selects whether heterogeneous heavy‐oil residues evolve into soft or hard carbon. Removing mobile, coking‐prone fractions before oxidation prevents surface self‐sealing and redirects the precursor toward homogeneous crosslinking and alveolar hard carbon. The closed‐cell architecture supports durable and wide‐temperature sodium storage, establishing precursor homogenization as an upstream design principle.








ABSTRACT
Competing with lithium‐ion technology on cost and resource abundance requires sodium‐ion batteries to use hard‐carbon anodes produced from abundant, inexpensive feedstocks without sacrificing structural control. Yet the natural and residual feedstocks that meet these requirements are typically chemically heterogeneous. Competing transformations among their constituent fractions before high‐temperature treatment make the carbonization pathway and carbon architecture difficult to predict and direct. Here, controlled fraction removal and reintroduction reveal a new mechanism whereby coking‐crosslinking competition selects the carbonization pathway. Surface coking blocks oxygen access and suppresses bulk crosslinking, whereas low‐temperature pre‐purification removes coking‐prone fractions, preserving an oxygen‐accessible skeleton that forms alveolar hard carbon (AHC). Operando x‐ray diffraction (XRD)/Raman and synchrotron x‐ray absorption near‐edge structure (XANES) establish that the low‐potential plateau arises from reversible formation of highly reduced sodium species within confined pores. AHC‐120@15‐1400 delivers 388.3 mAh g−1 with 91.3% initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE), retains 94.3% capacity after 10 500 cycles at 4 A g−1, and operates from −25°C to 45°C. A 1.2 Ah pouch cell retains 82.5% capacity after 1,000 cycles, while the route lowers cradle‐to‐gate material‐resource impact by 35.6% relative to commercial hard‐carbon production. Controlling coking‐crosslinking competition establishes a pathway‐selective design principle for converting heterogeneous carbon resources into durable, wide‐temperature sodium‐storage carbons.
